text: A Scrum Team has been working on a product for 9 Sprints. A new Product Owner who is new to Scrum joins the team and understands she is accountable for the Product Backlog. However, she is unsure about the purpose of the Product Backlog. She has read that the Product Backlog should be a list of all user features for the product. She goes to the Scrum Master asking where to put the other types of requirements that are going to be taken into account. Are all of the following types of requirements acceptable on a Product Backlog? Stability requirements. Performance requirements. Product Functionality. Documentation. Fixes. (choose the best answer)
options: Yes, they all belong on the Product Backlog. Product Backlog is supposed to be the Single Source of Truth for all the work for the product.

No, Product Backlog is a tool for the Product Owner. The Product Owner represents the users and stakeholders. Other types of requirements should be managed separately by the Developers. They are not the Product Owner's concern.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: yes, they all belong on the Product Backlog. The Product Backlog is the single source of all work for the product — functionality, fixes, documentation, and non-functional needs like stability and performance all go there. Keeping other requirement 'types' in separate lists would fragment transparency and break the emergent, ordered single source the whole team works from.

text: What variables should a Product Owner consider when ordering the Product Backlog? (choose the best answer)
options: Development cohesion as indicated by the Developers.
The availability of resources and skills for implementation.
Lowest development cost in order to maximize Return on Investment (ROI).
Effort first, then value.
Anything that informs them to achieve the product's goals and to optimize the value delivered.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: anything that helps achieve the product's goals and optimize value. Ordering is value-driven and holistic — the PO weighs value, risk, dependencies, and more. Resource availability, lowest cost, or effort-first ordering are narrow, traditional lenses that ignore the real aim: maximizing delivered value toward the Product Goal.

text: It is mandatory for the Product Owner to monitor and share progress of the Product Backlog by using which method? (choose the best answer)
options: A Product or Release burn-down chart.
A Value burn-up chart.
A Gantt Chart.
Any practice based on trends of work completed and upcoming work.
A Sprint Review acceptance report.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: any practice based on trends of work completed and upcoming work. Scrum mandates that progress be monitored and shared, but prescribes no specific tool — burn-downs, burn-ups, cumulative flow, or anything trend-based are all fine. A Gantt chart or an 'acceptance report' are not required, and no single technique is mandatory.

text: The Product Owner manages the Product Backlog. Who is accountable for estimating the effort to complete the Product Backlog Items? (choose the best answer)
options: The Developers.
The PMO.
The Product Owner.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the Developers. Those who will do the work size the work, so estimates reflect real capability. The Product Owner orders and clarifies but does not estimate for the team, and there is no PMO role in Scrum.

text: True or False: The Sprint Review is the only time at which stakeholder feedback is taken into account.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: False. The Sprint Review is a key feedback point, but stakeholder feedback is welcomed continuously — the Product Owner collaborates with stakeholders throughout, not only at the Review.

text: How do timeboxes help the Product Owner and the other members of the Scrum Team validate assumptions, adapt, and maximize the value of their product? (choose the best answer)
options: Timeboxes help by making sure a Sprint does not stop until all testing is done, and the work is verified by the Product Owner.
Timeboxes assure the Product Owner that the Developers will finish all work on the Sprint Backlog by the end of the Sprint.

Timeboxes help minimize risk by creating the opportunity to validate assumptions using feedback from users and the market; allowing Scrum Teams to inspect progress toward the Product Goal and decide whether to pivot or persevere.
At the end of each Sprint when the timebox expires a detailed report with all test cases and test results is available.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: timeboxes minimize risk by creating regular chances to validate assumptions with real user/market feedback, so the team can inspect progress toward the Product Goal and decide to pivot or persevere. Timeboxes are upper bounds for inspect-and-adapt — not guarantees that all work finishes or that a full test report drops at the end.

text: True or False: The value delivered by a product can only be determined by revenue.
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: False. Value is multi-dimensional — customer satisfaction, adoption, cost, risk reduction, and more — not revenue alone. Reducing value to a single financial figure misses much of what makes a product valuable.

text: True or False: The Scrum Team must choose at least one high priority process improvement item, identified during the Sprint Retrospective, and place it in the Sprint Backlog.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: False. The 2020 Scrum Guide dropped the old requirement to carry one improvement item into the next Sprint Backlog. Teams should act on improvements, but Scrum no longer mandates placing one in the Sprint Backlog.

text: How important is it for a Product Owner to order Product Backlog Items by using value points? (choose the best answer)
options: Calculating value points is a predictive approach that conflicts with the empiricism of Scrum, and is therefore not acceptable.
Using value points is the ultimate way for a Product Owner to predict the value that the product will provide.
The Product Owner may order the Product Backlog by using value points or select another technique, the decision is up to them.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the PO may use value points or any other technique — it's their choice. Scrum prescribes that the Product Backlog be ordered to maximize value, but not the method. Value points are neither forbidden nor the one true way; the ordering technique is left to the Product Owner.

text: When can the Product Backlog be updated? (choose the best answer)
options: Never, unless agreed to by the change request.
At any time when done by the Product Owner or a delegate.
Only after a Sprint Review if agreed to by the stakeholders.
Only during Product Backlog Refinement sessions if the Product Owner is present.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: at any time, by the Product Owner or a delegate. The Product Backlog is a living artifact updated continuously as insights emerge — it is not gated behind change requests, Sprint Reviews, stakeholder sign-off, or dedicated refinement sessions.

text: True or False: The Product Owner should have the entire Product Backlog documented in detail before the first Sprint can start?
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. The Product Backlog need not be fully documented before Sprint 1. It is emergent; you start with enough for a first Sprint and refine continuously. Big-upfront-requirements is exactly what Scrum avoids.

text: True or False: The Sprint Backlog is a result of Sprint Planning, and it includes the Sprint Goal.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: True. Sprint Planning produces the Sprint Backlog, which is composed of three things per the Scrum Guide 2020: the Sprint Goal (the why), the set of Product Backlog items selected (the what), and the plan for delivering them (the how). The Sprint Goal is therefore an integral part of the Sprint Backlog, not a separate artifact.

text: Who is accountable for creating a valuable and usable Increment each Sprint? (choose the best answer)
options: The Scrum Master.
The CEO.
The Developers.
The Scrum Team.
The Product Owner.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: The Scrum Team. Accountability for a valuable, usable Increment each Sprint sits with the whole Scrum Team, not a single role. The Developers do the building, but the Product Owner (value) and Scrum Master (effectiveness) are part of the same team and share accountability for the outcome. The CEO is external and has no Scrum accountability here.

text: What are two effective ways for the Scrum Team to make non-functional requirements visible? (choose the best two answers)
options: Run the integration and regression tests before the end of the Sprint, and capture the open work for the Sprint Backlog of the next Sprint.
Add them to the Product Backlog to ensure transparency.
Put them on a separate list on the Scrum board, available for all to see.
Add them to the Definition of Done so the work is taken care of every Sprint.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: add them to the Product Backlog, and add them to the Definition of Done. Non-functional requirements become transparent as ordered backlog items and, when they must hold every Sprint (e.g. performance, security), as DoD criteria enforced each Increment. A separate side-list fragments transparency, and deferring the work to next Sprint contradicts delivering a Done Increment.

text: The Cone of Uncertainty can be used to do what? (choose the best answer)
options: Determine the length of the next Sprint.
Determine the cost of a project before it begins.
Determine whether to cut quality, similar to the Iron Triangle of project management.
Illustrate that as a project forecast lengthens, it is increasingly less certain.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: it illustrates that the further out a forecast reaches, the less certain it is. The Cone of Uncertainty is a way to visualise diminishing predictability over time — it is an argument for empiricism and short feedback loops, not a tool to fix Sprint length, pre-compute cost, or trade quality (the Iron Triangle thinking Scrum rejects).

text: Which is NOT a valid consideration when ordering a Product Backlog? (choose the best answer)
options: Risk.
Tools and techniques.
Importance to customers.
Alignment with business strategy and goals.
Dependencies on other Product Backlog Items.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct (not a valid consideration): tools and techniques. Ordering is about value, risk, importance to customers, business-strategy alignment, and dependencies. The tools or techniques used to build an item don't determine where it sits in the order.

text: True or False: The Product Owner must write all of the Product Backlog Items (e.g. user stories, requirements, etc.) on the Product Backlog before handing them over to the Scrum Team.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. The Product Backlog is emergent and refined continuously; the PO does not have to write every item fully before the team engages. Items are elaborated collaboratively over time, just-in-time for selection.

text: Which of the following are criteria to order Product Backlog Items? (choose all that apply)
options: Value of Product Backlog Items.
Dependencies between Product Backlog Items.
Dependencies to other products.
The availability of the Scrum Master.
All of the above.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: value, dependencies between items, and dependencies to other products. These legitimately shape order. The Scrum Master's availability is irrelevant to ordering, and 'all of the above' would wrongly include it.

text: All Scrum artifacts must be transparent to ensure sufficient accuracy of inspection. Which two measures ensure that the Product Backlog is transparent? (choose the best two answers)
options: The Product Backlog is managed using a web-based tool.
The Product Backlog is available to all stakeholders.
The Product Backlog is ordered.
Each Product Backlog Item has a MoSCoW priority.
The Product Backlog only has work for the next 2 Sprints.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Product Backlog is available to all stakeholders, and it is ordered. Transparency comes from visibility and a meaningful order that reflects priorities. The specific tool, a MoSCoW scheme, or limiting the backlog to two Sprints are not what create transparency.

text: Why is it important that there is only one Product Owner per product? (choose the best three answers)
options: The Scrum Team always knows who determines the order of the Product Backlog.
The Scrum Master knows who acts as their backup while on vacation.
It is clear who is accountable for the ultimate value of the product.
It would confuse the stakeholders if they had to work with more than one person.
It helps avoid barriers to effective communication and rapid decision-making.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: it's clear who is accountable for the product's ultimate value; and it avoids barriers to effective communication and rapid decision-making (and the team always knows who orders the backlog). A single PO gives clear accountability and fast decisions — not merely to avoid confusing stakeholders or to arrange vacation cover.

text: Which of the following practices might help the Product Owner minimize waste in developing and sustaining the Product Backlog? (choose the best two answers)
options: Avoid distracting the Scrum Team by maintaining newly gathered Product Backlog items in a separate Product Backlog until they are fully understood.
Only fully describe Product Backlog items when it seems likely they will be implemented.
Hand off ownership of the Product Backlog to someone else.
Remove items from the Product Backlog that have not been addressed in a long time.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: only fully describe items when they're likely to be implemented, and remove long-untouched items. Both reduce waste from elaborating or storing work that may never be built. Keeping a separate hidden backlog or handing off ownership don't reduce waste — they fragment or abdicate it.

text: True or False: Product Owners must create clear and unambiguous acceptance criteria for each Product Backlog Item before it may be selected in Sprint Planning.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. Acceptance criteria are useful but not a Scrum precondition for selecting an item at Sprint Planning. The Developers decide what they can forecast; Scrum does not mandate complete, unambiguous criteria first.

text: What three things might a Scrum Product Owner focus on to ensure the product delivers value? (choose the best three answers)
options: Minimizing changes to project scope.
How much of the functionality of the product is being used.
How quickly or easily the product can be absorbed and used by its customers.
Direct customer feedback.
Velocity is increasing over time.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: how much functionality is actually used; how quickly/easily customers can absorb and use it; and direct customer feedback. Value is measured by real outcomes and adoption. Minimizing scope change and rising velocity are internal/plan-focused signals, not value.

text: How often should customer satisfaction be measured? (choose the best answer)
options: Quarterly.
Annually.
Daily.
Frequently.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: frequently. Customer satisfaction should be measured often so the team can adapt quickly — not on a fixed quarterly or annual cadence, and not necessarily daily. Frequency supports empiricism.

text: Why would you expect a Product Owner to care that the Scrum Team adheres to its Definition of Done? (choose the best two answers)
options: To be able to punish the team when they do not meet their velocity goal for the Sprint.
The Product Owner should not care about the Definition of Done, it is the Scrum Team's responsibility.
The Definition of Done can affect the product's total cost of ownership.
To have complete transparency into what has been done at the end of each Sprint.
To forecast the team's productivity over time.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the DoD can affect the product's total cost of ownership, and it gives complete transparency into what has been Done. A PO cares about quality because weak 'Done' creates hidden debt and untrustworthy Increments. It is not a tool to punish the team or a mere productivity forecast.

text: A product's success is measured by: (choose the best three answers)
options: The impact on customer satisfaction.
The impact on cost.
The impact on my boss's mood.
The delivery of upfront defend scope compared to the upfront planned time.
The impact on my performance rating.
The impact on revenue.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: customer satisfaction, cost, and revenue. Product success is measured by the value and outcomes it delivers to customers and the business, not by internal or vanity signals. 'My boss's mood', 'my performance rating', and 'planned scope delivered on planned time' are outputs/opinions, not measures of value — the last one is exactly the traditional plan-conformance thinking Scrum moves away from.

text: True or False: Dependencies could influence how the Product Owner orders Product Backlog Items.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: True. Dependencies (between items or on other products/teams) are a legitimate factor the Product Owner weighs when ordering the Product Backlog.

text: Scrum is based on empiricism. All of its artifacts must be transparent to ensure sufficient accuracy of inspection. How can the Scrum Team maintain the Product Backlog to maximize its transparency? (choose the best answer)
options: The Product Backlog is only updated at a release planning meeting with the stakeholders and the change control board present.
Product Backlog Items must be sized such that the highest ordered items are no bigger than a Sprint.
The Product Backlog is only updated at the Sprint Review, when both the Scrum Team and the stakeholders are available.
Product Backlog Items should hold no more than 8 points of work, which is the average in the range of acceptable sizes of 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and 13.
The Product Backlog is continually kept up to date with the most recent insights.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Product Backlog is continually kept up to date with the most recent insights. Transparency for empiricism means the artifact reflects reality at all times, so it must be updated continuously as things are learned — not frozen until a review or change-control meeting. Fixed point-size rules and rigid update cadences are practices Scrum does not prescribe.

text: What is the responsibility of the Product Owner in crafting the Sprint Goal? (choose the best answer)
options: The Product Owner has no responsibility in it. This is the Developers responsibility.
The Product Owner defines the scope for a Sprint and therefore also the Sprint Goal.
The Product Owner should not come to the Sprint Planning without a clearly defined Sprint Goal.
The Product Owner should come to the Sprint Planning with a business objective in mind and work with the Developers to craft the Sprint Goal.
The Product Owner must work with stakeholders to set each Sprint's Goal.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the PO comes to Planning with a business objective and works with the Developers to craft the Sprint Goal. The Goal is a collaboration — the PO neither has 'no responsibility', nor unilaterally defines it, nor must arrive with it fully formed, nor sets it with stakeholders.

text: When should the Product Owner update the project plan? (choose the best answer)
options: The Product Backlog is the plan in Scrum. It is updated as new information and insights emerge.
The project plan must be updated prior to the Sprint Retrospective.
Before the Sprint Planning to know how much work will have to be done in the Sprint.
After the Daily Scrum to ensure an accurate daily overview of project progress.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the Product Backlog IS the plan in Scrum, updated as new information emerges. There is no separate 'project plan' to maintain on a schedule tied to the Retrospective, Planning, or Daily Scrum.

text: A Product Backlog is: (choose the best three answers)
options: Managed by the Product Owner.
Only visible to the Product Owner and stakeholders.
An exhaustive list of upfront approved requirements to be implemented.
Ordered based on priority, value, dependencies, and risk.
An inventory of things to be done for the Product.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: managed by the Product Owner; ordered by priority, value, dependencies and risk; and an inventory of what needs doing for the product. It is not PO-and-stakeholder-only, nor an exhaustive, pre-approved, fixed requirements list — it is emergent and evolving.

text: How much time must a Product Owner spend with the Developers? (choose the best answer)
options: As much time as the Developers ask the Product Owner to be present.
Enough so that the Product Owner is confident, the Increment will meet the intended value.
40%, or more if the stakeholders agree.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: enough that the PO is confident the Increment will meet the intended value. Time with the Developers is driven by value assurance, not a fixed percentage or being at the Developers' beck and call. It needn't be 100% or a set 40%.

text: Which metrics will help a Product Owner determine if a product delivering value? (choose the best two answers)
options: Velocity.
Productivity.
Time to market.
Customer satisfaction.
Percentage of scope implemented.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: time to market and customer satisfaction. These reflect real delivered value. Velocity, productivity, and percentage of scope implemented are internal output measures, not value measures.

text: True or False: All planned work for the Product done by the Scrum Team must originate from the Product Backlog.
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: True. All work the Scrum Team does on the product should originate from the Product Backlog, the single source of truth. Work that bypasses it undermines transparency and the Product Owner's value ordering.

text: What typically happens if the Product Backlog is not sufficiently clear at Sprint Planning? (choose the best answer)
options: The Product Owner should select the Sprint Goal for the Scrum Team so that work can begin.
The Developers will find it difficult to create a Sprint forecast they are confident they can meet.
Nothing in particular.
The Scrum Master should not allow this to happen. Look for a new Scrum Master and restart the Sprint.
Sprint Planning is cancelled so refinement can be done first.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Developers will struggle to create a forecast they're confident in. Unclear backlog items make it hard to commit to a Sprint Goal. The PO doesn't dictate the Sprint Goal alone, refinement isn't a reason to cancel Planning, and replacing the Scrum Master isn't the remedy.

text: True or False: During the Sprint Review the stakeholder's role is to reorder the Product Backlog.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: False. Stakeholders provide feedback and input at the Sprint Review, but they do not reorder the Product Backlog — that is the Product Owner's accountability.

text: True or False: A Product Owner can measure success by an increase in the team's velocity.
options: True.
False.
trap: Velocity is not a measure of product value or cross-team performance.
explanation: Correct: False. Velocity is a capacity indicator, not a measure of success or value. A rising velocity can even accompany falling value; success is measured by outcomes for users and the business.

text: What might indicate to a Product Owner that she needs to work more with the Scrum Team? (choose the best answer)
options: People leave the Scrum Team.
She is not working fulltime with the Scrum Team.
The acceptance criteria do not appear to be complete.
The Increment presented at the Sprint Review does not reflect what she thought she had asked for.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the Increment at the Sprint Review doesn't reflect what she thought she asked for. That gap signals a communication/collaboration problem needing closer PO-team work. Staffing changes, part-time availability, or incomplete criteria are weaker signals than a mismatched Increment.

text: What are two effective ways for a Scrum Team to ensure security concerns are satisfied? (choose the best two answers)
options: Delegate the work to the security department.
Postpone the work until a specialist can perform a security audit and create a list of security-related Product Backlog Items.
Add security concerns to the Definition of Done.
Add a Sprint to specifically resolve all security concerns.
Have the Scrum Team create Product Backlog Items for each concern.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: add security concerns to the Definition of Done, and have the team create Product Backlog items for each concern. Security is built in every Sprint (DoD) and made transparent as backlog work. Delegating to a security department, waiting for a specialist audit, or a dedicated 'security Sprint' all push quality outside the Sprint.

text: You are the Scrum Master for four Scrum Teams working from the same Product Backlog. Several of the Developers come to you complaining that work identified for the upcoming two Sprints will require full-time commitment from a specialist who is external to the teams. What should the Scrum Master consider in this situation? (choose the best two answers)
options: The need to have enough work to keep all Developers busy.
The ability of the Scrum Teams to produce integrated Increments.
The desire to maintain a stable velocity.
The benefit of Developers figuring out a solution for themselves.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the ability of the teams to produce integrated Increments, and the benefit of Developers solving it themselves. A shared external specialist threatens integration and self-management. 'Keeping everyone busy' and 'stable velocity' are utilization/predictability concerns Scrum doesn't optimize for.

text: In order to maximize the value of the product, a Product Owner needs awareness of the following: (choose the best answer)
options: Competitive reasearch.
Customer feedback.
Product vision.
Forecasting & feasibility
All of the above.
None of the above.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: all of the above — competitive research, customer feedback, product vision, and forecasting/feasibility. Maximizing value requires the PO to hold all of these perspectives together, not just one.

text: The Developers ask their Product Owner to re-order the Product Backlog. The team is waiting for an external supplier to deliver a component. Without that component there will not be enough work in the next Sprint to occupy the full team. As the Scrum Master, what advice would you give the Product Owner? (choose the best answer)
options: Tell the Product Owner that the Product Backog should be ordered to maximize utilization of the Developers.
Tell the Product Owner to re-order the Product Backlog so the work involving the external component can be planned in a separate Sprint.
Remind the Product Owner that their primary concern is the flow of value reflected in the ordering of the Product Backlog.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: remind the PO that their primary concern is the flow of value in the ordering — not Developer utilization. Ordering to keep the team busy, or to shuffle the external-component work into a separate Sprint for utilization's sake, subordinates value to busyness, which inverts the Product Owner's purpose.

text: A Project Manager working with your Scrum Team has raised concerns about progress and money spent. What are the two best responses? (choose the best two answers)
options: Show the Earned Value Analysis (EVA) report.
Scrum does not have Project Managers so disregard their concerns.
Promote transparency by sharing the Product Backlog and ensuring the Project Manager has access.
Share the last stakeholder briefing document prepared by the Product Owner.
Have a discussion with the Project Manager, share the current impediments and forecast for the Sprint.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: promote transparency by sharing the Product Backlog with the Project Manager, and have a direct conversation sharing impediments and the Sprint forecast. Transparency and dialogue address the concern honestly. Dismissing the person because 'Scrum has no PM', or reaching for EVA reports, doesn't build trust or reflect Scrum's empiricism.

text: The Product Owner is the person who will be held accountable if a product does not achieve its goals or deliver value. Does this mean that the Product Owner has final say over the Definition of Done? (choose the best answer)
options: Yes, the Product Owner decides the Definition of Done. The Developers may be consulted.
No, the Scrum Team decides the Definition of Done. The Product Owner is just one member of the Scrum Team.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: no — the Scrum Team decides the Definition of Done; the PO is one member of that team. Even though the PO is accountable for value, the DoD is not theirs to dictate; it's owned collaboratively (within any organizational standard).

text: Which statement best describes Scrum? (choose the best answer)
options: A defined and predictive process that conforms to the principles of Scientific Management.
A framework to generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems.
A cookbook that defines best practices for software development.
A complete methodology that defines how to develop software.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: a framework to generate value through adaptive solutions for complex problems — the Scrum Guide 2020's own definition. Scrum is deliberately not a predictive process, a cookbook of best practices, or a complete software methodology; it is a lightweight framework you wrap your own practices around.

text: What is a Product Owner typically responsible for during a Sprint? (choose the best two answers)
options: Nothing.
Working with the Scrum Team on Product Backlog Refinement.
Attending every Daily Scrum to answer questions about the Sprint Backlog items.
Updating the work plan for the Developers on a daily basis.
Collaborating with stakeholders, users and customers.
Creating financial reporting upon the spent hours reported by the Developers.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: working with the Scrum Team on Product Backlog refinement, and collaborating with stakeholders, users and customers. These are core PO activities during a Sprint. The PO isn't idle, isn't required at every Daily, doesn't plan the Developers' daily work, and doesn't produce hours-based financial reports.

text: True or False: Product Owners must specify complete acceptance criteria for a Product Backlog Item before the Developers can select the item in Sprint Planning.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. Complete acceptance criteria are not required before Developers may select an item. Items need enough shared understanding to forecast — not exhaustive criteria — and understanding continues to emerge during the Sprint.

text: Who is accountable for tracking the remaining work toward the Sprint Goal? (choose the best answer)
options: The Scrum Master.
The Developers.
The Project Manager.
The Product Owner.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Developers. They own the Sprint Backlog and are accountable for tracking their remaining work toward the Sprint Goal (e.g. via any practice they choose, such as a burn-down). The Scrum Master and Product Owner support but do not track the Developers' progress; there is no Project Manager role in Scrum.

text: The Scrum Team should have all the skills needed to: (choose the best answer)
options: Complete the project within the date and cost as calculated by the Product Owner.
Turn Product Backlog Items into a valuable, useful Increment.
Do all of the development work, except for specialized testing that requires additional tools and environments.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: turn Product Backlog items into a valuable, useful Increment. A Scrum Team has all the skills needed to create value each Sprint — including all testing. Delivering to a PO-calculated date/cost, or excluding specialized testing, contradicts cross-functionality and Done every Sprint.

text: Which three of the following are timeboxed events in Scrum? (choose the best three answers)
options: Sprint 0.
Release Retrospective.
Sprint Retrospective.
Daily Scrum.
Sprint Planning.
Release Planning.
Sprint Testing.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: Sprint Retrospective, Daily Scrum, Sprint Planning. These are three of the five timeboxed events (the Sprint itself, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective). 'Sprint 0', 'Release Planning/Retrospective', and 'Sprint Testing' are not Scrum events — they are traditional add-ons Scrum does not define.

text: Who starts the Daily Scrum? (choose the best answer)
options: The person who has the token.
Whoever the Developers decide should start.
The person coming in last. This encourages people to be on time and helps to stay within the timebox.
The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master. This ensures that the Developers have the event, and it stays within the timebox.
trap: The Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
explanation: Correct: whoever the Developers decide should start. The Daily Scrum belongs to the Developers, who self-manage how they run it, including who kicks it off. Gimmicks like 'the last person in' or having the Scrum Master/Product Owner run it contradict Developer self-management.

text: Which of the following services are appropriate for a Scrum Master in regard to the Daily Scrum? (choose the best answer)
options: Lead the discussions.
Make sure that all 3 questions have been answered by each member of the team.
Keep track of whether each Developer has a chance to speak.
Teach the Developers to keep the Daily Scrum within 15 minutes.
All of the above.
trap: The Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
explanation: Correct: teach the Developers to keep the Daily Scrum within 15 minutes. The Scrum Master coaches and supports self-management; they don't lead the Daily, police three questions, or track speaking turns — those undermine the Developers' ownership of the event.

text: True or False: Sprint Reviews are an opportunity to collect stakeholder feedback.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: True. The Sprint Review is explicitly an opportunity to inspect the Increment with stakeholders and collect their feedback to adapt the Product Backlog.

text: Who is on the Scrum Team? (choose all that apply)
options: Scrum Master.
Product Owner.
Developers.
Project Manager.
None of the above.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: Scrum Master, Product Owner, and Developers. The Scrum Team is exactly these three accountabilities, with no sub-teams or hierarchies. There is no Project Manager in Scrum.

text: What tactic should a Scrum Master use to divide a group of 100 people into multiple Scrum Teams? (choose the best answer)
options: Ask the people to divide themselves into teams.
Create teams based on their skills across multiple layers (such as database, UI, etc.).
Ask the Product Owner to assign the people to teams.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: ask the people to divide themselves into teams. Self-organization into teams reflects Scrum's values and self-management. Forming teams by technical layer, or having the PO assign people, imposes structure and undercuts ownership.

text: Which of the following are true about the length of the Sprint? (choose the best answer)
options: The length of the Sprint should be proportional to the work that is done in between Sprints.
Sprint length is determined during Sprint Planning, and should hold the time it will take to code the planned features in the upcoming Sprint, but does not include time for any testing.
Sprint length is determined during Sprint Planning, and should be long enough to make sure the Scrum Team can deliver what is to be accomplished in the upcoming Sprint.
All Sprints must be one month or less.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: all Sprints must be one month or less. The only fixed rule is the maximum timebox of one month; shorter Sprints create more feedback loops and lower risk. Sprint length is not stretched to fit planned work, and testing is never excluded from a Sprint — every Sprint must produce a Done Increment.

text: Which are appropriate topics for discussion in a Sprint Retrospective? (choose the best three answers)
options: Definition of Done.
Arranging the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint.
How the Scrum Team does its work.
Team relations.
The value of work currently represented in the Product Backlog.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Definition of Done, how the Scrum Team does its work, and team relations. The Retrospective inspects people, relationships, process, and tools — including the DoD — to improve effectiveness. Arranging next Sprint's backlog happens in Sprint Planning, and assessing Product Backlog value happens at the Sprint Review, not here.

text: True or False: The Product Owner makes sure the correct stakeholders are invited to the Sprint Retrospective. They might have important instructions for team improvements.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. The Sprint Retrospective is for the Scrum Team to improve itself; stakeholders are not invited, and they do not hand the team 'instructions' for improvement.

text: Who has the final decision about the order of items in the Product Backlog? (choose the best answer)
options: The Scrum Team.
The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master.
The Stakeholders.
The Developers.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Product Owner. The PO has the final say on Product Backlog order and is accountable for it. They may take input from many sources, but the decision is theirs — not the Developers', Scrum Master's, or stakeholders'.

text: What are the two primary ways a Scrum Master helps a Scrum Team work at its highest level of productivity? (choose the best two answers)
options: By ensuring the meetings start and end at the proper time.
By facilitating Scrum Team decisions.
By keeping high value features high in the Product Backlog.
By removing impediments that hinder the Scrum Team.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: by facilitating Scrum Team decisions, and by removing impediments. These directly raise the team's effectiveness. Starting/ending meetings on time is minor, and keeping high-value features high in the backlog is the Product Owner's job, not the Scrum Master's.

text: During a Sprint, when is new work or further decomposition of work added to the Sprint Backlog? (choose the best answer)
options: When the Product Owner identifies new work.
When the Scrum Master has time to enter it.
As soon as possible after it is identified.
During the Daily Scrum after the Developers approve it.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: as soon as possible after it is identified. The Sprint Backlog is emergent; the Developers update it throughout the Sprint the moment new work or decomposition becomes known, to keep it transparent. It doesn't wait for the PO, the Scrum Master, or a Daily Scrum approval step.

text: True or False: A high-performance Scrum Team ensures that each Increment is complete by running a Release Sprint.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: False. Scrum requires a Done Increment every Sprint, so a separate 'Release Sprint' to complete quality is an anti-pattern. Quality is built in continuously via the Definition of Done, not bolted on at the end.

text: The Developers select a set of Product Backlog Items for a Sprint Backlog with the intent to get the selected items done by the end of the Sprint. Which three phrases best describe the purpose of a Definition of Done? (choose the best three answers)
options: It tracks the percentage complete of a Product Backlog Item.
It defines what it takes for an Increment to be ready for release.
It creates transparency over the work inspected at the Sprint Review.
It guides the Developers in creating a forecast at the Sprint Planning.
It provides a template for elements that need to be included in the documentation.
It controls whether the Developers have performed their tasks.
trap: Done is defined by the Definition of Done, not by acceptance or partial completion.
explanation: Correct: it defines what it takes for an Increment to be ready for release; it creates transparency over the work inspected at the Sprint Review; and it guides Developers when forecasting at Planning. The DoD is a quality/transparency standard — not a percent-complete tracker, a documentation template, or a task-compliance check.

text: What are three benefits of self-management? (choose the best three answers)
options: Increased self-accountability.
Increased rule compliance.
Increased creativity.
Increased commitment.
Increased accuracy of estimates.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: increased self-accountability, creativity, and commitment. Owning decisions raises accountability, sparks creative solutions, and deepens buy-in. Self-management is not about tighter rule compliance or more accurate estimates.

text: A new Developer is having continuing conflicts with existing members of the Scrum Team, which is impacting the delivery of the Increment. If necessary, who is responsible for removing the Developer from the Scrum Team? (choose the best answer)
options: The hiring manager is responsible, they hired the Developer.
The Product Owner is responsible, they control the return on investment (ROI).
The Scrum Team is responsible.
The Scrum Master is responsible, they remove impediments.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Scrum Team is responsible. A self-managing team decides its own membership questions, including, if truly necessary, removing a member. It's not the hiring manager's, PO's, or Scrum Master's call.

text: A Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product that is the result of the work of the Scrum Team. Which of the following can be delegated to others, while the Product Owner remains accountable for the work? (choose the best two answers)
options: Attending the Sprint Review.
Ordering Product Backlog Items.
Developing and communicating the Product Goal.
Attending the Sprint Retrospective.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: ordering Product Backlog items, and developing/communicating the Product Goal. A PO may delegate this work but stays accountable. Attending the Sprint Review/Retrospective are their own participation as a team member, not delegable 'work' in the same sense.

text: During a Sprint Retrospective, the Developers propose moving the Daily Scrum to only occur on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Which two are the most appropriate responses for the Scrum Master to recommend? (choose the best two answers)
options: Consider the request and decide on which days the Daily Scrum should occur.
Coach the team on why the Daily Scrum is important as an opportunity to update the plan.
Acknowledge and support the self-managing team's decision.
Have the Developers vote.
Learn why the Developers want this and work with them to improve the outcome of the Daily Scrum.
trap: The Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
explanation: Correct: coach the team on why the Daily Scrum matters as a chance to update the plan, and learn why they want the change and work with them to improve the event. The Scrum Master neither decides the days nor rubber-stamps a change that weakens a daily inspect-and-adapt loop — they help the team improve the underlying issue.

text: During the Sprint Retrospective a Scrum Team has identified several high priority process improvements. Which of the following statements is most accurate? (choose the best answer)
options: The Scrum Team may add the items to the Sprint Backlog for the next Sprint.
The Scrum Team should choose at least one high priority process improvement to place in the Product Backlog.
The Scrum Team should decline to add a process improvement to the Sprint Backlog when things are running smoothly.
The Scrum Master selects the most important process improvement and places it in the Sprint Backlog.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Scrum Team may add the improvement items to the next Sprint Backlog. The 2020 guide makes this optional, not mandatory — they may include improvements, but aren't required to carry one, and the Scrum Master doesn't unilaterally select or place them.

text: How is management that is external to the Scrum Team involved in the Daily Scrum? (choose the best answer)
options: The Product Owner represents their opinions.
Managers are not required at the Daily Scrum.
The Scrum Master speaks on their behalf.
Management gives an update at the start of each Daily Scrum.
trap: The Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
explanation: Correct: managers are not required at the Daily Scrum. It is by and for the Developers; external management has no role inside it. The PO/Scrum Master don't 'represent' management there, and management doesn't give updates — their support to the team happens outside team events.

text: How much time is required after a Sprint to prepare for the next Sprint? (choose the best answer)
options: The break between Sprints is timeboxed to one-week for a one-month Sprint, and usually less for shorter Sprints.
Enough time for the requirements for the next Sprint to be determined and documented.
Enough time for the Developers to finish the testing from the last Sprint.
None. A new Sprint starts immediately following the end of the previous Sprint.
All of the above are allowed depending on the situation.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: none — a new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one ends. Scrum has no gap, 'Sprint 0', or hardening/prep period between Sprints. Refinement and readiness happen continuously inside Sprints, not in a break between them.

text: How much work is required of the Developers to complete a Product Backlog Item selected during the Sprint Planning? (choose the best answer)
options: As much as they can fit into the Sprint, with remaining work deferred to the next Sprint.
As much as is required to meet the Scrum Team's Definition of Done.
All development work and at least some testing.
A proportional amount of time on analysis, design, development, and testing.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: as much as is required to meet the team's Definition of Done. An item isn't finished until it satisfies the DoD — not just 'as much as fits', 'development plus some testing', or a fixed split of analysis/design/dev/test time.

text: How often should Scrum Team membership change? (choose the best answer)
options: Every Sprint to promote shared learning.
As needed, with no special allowance for changes in productivity.
Never, it reduces productivity.
As needed, while taking into account a short-term reduction in productivity.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: as needed, while accounting for a short-term dip in productivity. Membership can change when necessary, but changes temporarily reduce productivity as the team re-forms. It's neither forced every Sprint nor forbidden forever.

text: If Product Backlog Refinement is needed, when is the ideal time for refinement to take place and who should participate? (choose the best two answers)
options: Business analysts in the organization should do this work for the Scrum Team 1-2 Sprints ahead of the development Sprints.
The Product Owner must do this as essential work in Sprint 0.
The Scrum Team on an ongoing basis, defining Product Backlog Items into smaller more precise items that are ready for selection.
The Scrum Team during the current Sprint, if they have been unable during preceding Sprints to define Product Backlog Items with enough precision to begin work.
The Product Owner takes the time between the end of one Sprint and the start of the next Sprint to complete refinement.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Scrum Team refines on an ongoing basis, breaking items into ready ones; and does so during the current Sprint if prior refinement was insufficient. Refinement is continuous team work — not something business analysts do ahead in 'Sprint 0', nor a between-Sprint PO task.

text: Scrum requires that the Product Owner must use which of the following items? (choose all that apply)
options: Burndown chart.
Feature burn-up.
Critical Path Analysis.
Project Gantt Chart.
None of the above.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: none of the above. Scrum mandates no specific artifact or chart — not burndowns, burn-ups, critical path, or Gantt charts. The PO chooses whatever practice makes progress transparent.

text: True or False: A Product Owner with multiple teams working on one product should maintain separate Product Backlogs for each team.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. One product means one Product Backlog, even with multiple teams. Separate per-team backlogs fragment the product view and break transparency.

text: True or False: The Scrum Team is accountable for releasing the most valuable product.
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: False. The Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable Increment every Sprint; the Product Owner specifically is accountable for maximizing value and deciding on release. 'Releasing the most valuable product' isn't phrased as a whole-team accountability.

text: What are three advantages of a Product Owner sharing a clearly defined Product Goal with the Scrum Team? (choose the best three answers)
options: It helps the Scrum Team keep focus and they can weigh any decision against the Product Goal.
It helps the Developers estimate the date that the Product Backlog will be complete.
It is easier to inspect Incremental progress at the Sprint Review.
It is not mandatory in Scrum. There is no real advantage.
It provides a good overall direction so Sprints will feel less like isolated pieces of work.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: it keeps the team focused so decisions can be weighed against the Product Goal; it makes Incremental progress easier to inspect at the Review; and it gives overall direction so Sprints feel connected. A Product Goal is not for predicting a 'backlog-complete' date, and it is genuinely advantageous (contrary to the 'no advantage' option).

text: Which approach is best for Scrum Teams in order to produce valuable Increments? (choose the best answer)
options: Each Developer works on the component where they feel that they can contribute.
Each Scrum Team is accountable for developing functionality from beginning to end.
Each Scrum Team works on an independent set of components.
Each Scrum Member works only as an independent layer of the system.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: each Scrum Team develops functionality end-to-end. Cross-functional, feature-oriented teams produce integrated value. Working by individual component, independent component sets, or single-layer specialists creates hand-offs and integration risk.

text: Who is accountable for managing the progress of work during a Sprint? (choose the best answer)
options: The Product Owner.
The Developers.
The most junior member of the team.
The Scrum Master.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Developers. They self-manage the day-to-day work needed to meet the Sprint Goal and are accountable for managing their own progress during the Sprint. The Scrum Master fosters effectiveness and the Product Owner manages value, but neither manages the Developers' work.

text: Who is part of the discussion about which Product Backlog Items are selected for a Sprint? (choose the best answer)
options: The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master.
The Scrum Team.
The Developers.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Scrum Team. Selecting items for a Sprint is a collaborative Scrum Team activity — the PO brings the goal and priorities, the Developers decide what they can forecast. It's not the PO alone, the Scrum Master, or only the Developers in isolation.

text: Why does the Product Owner want the Developers to adhere to its Definition of Done? (choose the best answer)
options: To predict the teams productivity over time.
To have complete transparency into what has been done at the end of each Sprint.
To know what the team will deliver over the next three Sprints.
To be able to reprimand the team when they do not meet their velocity goal for the Sprint.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: to have complete transparency into what has been done at the end of each Sprint. A shared Definition of Done tells everyone, including the Product Owner, exactly what 'Done' means, so the Increment's state is transparent and can be trusted. It is not a productivity forecast or a tool to reprimand the team.

text: Your management has asked you to take the lead in the development of a new product. Six teams new to Scrum will build this product. You have gathered a number of requirements and ideas into an early form of a Product Backlog. How would you minimize dependencies between the Scrum Teams? (choose the best answer)
options: You work with the Developers on how to best analyze and break apart the work.
You divide Product Backlog Items among the six Product Owners.
You create an independent Product Backlog per Scrum Team.
You identify the dependencies and re-order the Product Backlog for the other five Product Owners.
You raise this as an impediment with the Scrum Master.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: work with the Developers on how best to analyze and break apart the work. Those doing the work reduce dependencies most effectively by shaping how it's split. Splitting the backlog across six POs, giving each team its own backlog, or re-ordering for other POs all fragment the single product view.

text: What does it mean to say that an event has a timebox? (choose the best answer)
options: The event must take at least a minimum amount of time.
The event must happen at a set time.
The event can take no more than a maximum amount of time.
The event must happen by a given time.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the event can take no more than a maximum amount of time. A timebox sets an upper bound; the event can finish early once its purpose is met, but never runs over. It doesn't set a minimum duration or a fixed clock time.

text: True or False: A Scrum Master fulfills the same role as a traditional Project Manager.
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: False. A Scrum Master is a leader who serves the team and fosters effectiveness — not a Project Manager who directs, assigns, and controls. Equating the two is a common misconception.

text: When is it most appropriate for a Scrum Team to change the Definition of Done? (choose the best answer)
options: Prior to starting a new project.
During the Sprint Retrospective.
During Product Backlog Refinement.
During Sprint Planning.
trap: Done is defined by the Definition of Done, not by acceptance or partial completion.
explanation: Correct: during the Sprint Retrospective. Because the Retrospective inspects and improves how the team works — including quality standards — it is the natural moment to evolve the DoD (to take effect the next Sprint), not mid-Sprint at Planning or refinement.

text: True or False: A Product Owner should measure product value by the increase in the team's velocity.
options: True.
False.
trap: Velocity is not a measure of product value or cross-team performance.
explanation: Correct: False. Product value should not be measured by velocity. Velocity reflects team capacity, not the value users and the business receive.

text: Why do the Developers need a Sprint Goal? (choose the best answer)
options: The Developers are more focused with a common yet specific goal.
Sprint Goals are not valuable. Everything is known from the Product Backlog.
A Sprint Goal only gives purpose to Sprint 0.
Sprint Goal ensures that all of the Product Backlog Items selected for the Sprint are implemented.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: a common, specific goal creates focus. The Sprint Goal gives the Developers coherence and lets them self-manage toward one objective and adapt scope as needed. It is valuable (contrary to the distractors), applies to every Sprint, and does not guarantee all selected items get built.

text: Who creates a Product Backlog Item's estimate? (choose the best answer)
options: The Scrum Master.
The Product Owner with input from the Developers.
The Developers after clarifying requirements with the Product Owner.
The most senior people in the organization, including architects and subject matter experts.
The Developers, alone.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Developers, after clarifying requirements with the Product Owner. Those doing the work estimate it, using PO clarification to understand scope. Not the Scrum Master, not the PO estimating for them, and not senior architects imposing numbers.

text: True or False: Every Scrum Team must have a Product Owner and a Scrum Master.
options: False, a Scrum Master is only required when asked for by the Developers.
True, outcomes are affected by their participation and availability.
True, each must be 100% dedicated to their Scrum Team.
False, a Product Owner can be replaced by a Business Analyst among Developer.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: True — outcomes are affected by their participation and availability. Every Scrum Team has one PO and one Scrum Master; both accountabilities are needed. They needn't be 100% dedicated, and a Business Analyst cannot substitute for a Product Owner.

text: Which topics should be discussed in the Sprint Review? (choose the best answer)
options: The Scrum process, and how it was used during the Sprint.
Coding and engineering practices.
The product Increment.
All of the above.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the product Increment. The Sprint Review inspects the Increment and the state of the product/market to decide what to do next. Reviewing the Scrum process is the Retrospective's job, and engineering practices are not the focus of the Review.

text: Five new Scrum Teams have been created to build one product. A few of the Developers on one of the Scrum Teams ask the Scrum Master who will coordinate the work with the other teams. What should the Scrum Master do? (choose the best answer)
options: Collect the Sprint tasks from the teams at the end of their Sprint Planning and merge that into a consolidated plan for the entire Sprint.
Teach them that it is their responsibility to work with the other teams to create an Increment that is inclusive of all five team's work.
Teach the Product Owner to work with the Lead Developer on ordering Product Backlog in a way to avoid too much overlap during a Sprint.
Visit the five teams each day to inspect that their Sprint Backlogs are aligned.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: teach the Developers that coordinating with the other teams is their own responsibility. Self-managing teams working one product integrate and coordinate directly. Merging plans centrally, having a chief PO order to avoid overlap, or daily inspection tours all impose external control.

text: True or False: Cross-functional teams are optimized to work on one component or layer of a system only.
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: False. Cross-functional means the opposite — the team has all the skills to deliver end-to-end value, not to work on a single component or layer. Component/layer specialization is a hand-off anti-pattern.

text: What are two responsibilities of Testers in a Scrum Team? (choose the best two answers)
options: Tracking quality metrics.
Scrum has no "Tester" role.
Verifying the work of programmers.
The Developers are responsible for quality.
Finding bugs.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: Scrum has no 'Tester' role, and the Developers are responsible for quality. Everyone building the Increment is a 'Developer'; quality is a shared, whole-team responsibility rather than one person's job of finding bugs or verifying others' work.

text: Which two ways of creating Scrum Teams are consistent with Scrum's values? (choose the best two answers)
options: Existing teams propose how they would like to go about organizing into the new structure.
Bring all people together and let them organize into Scrum Teams.
Managers personally re-assign current subordinates to new teams.
The chief Product Owner determines the new team structure and assignments.
Managers collaborate to assign individuals into specific teams.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: existing teams propose how to reorganize, and all people come together and self-organize into teams. Both honor self-management and Scrum's values. Managers or a chief PO assigning individuals to teams imposes structure from outside.

text: True or False: The Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable Increment every Sprint.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: True. The Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, usable Increment every single Sprint — this is a core commitment of the framework.

text: When does the next Sprint begin? (choose the best answer)
options: The Monday following the Sprint Review.
Immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint.
Immediately following the next Sprint Planning.
When the Product Owner is ready.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint. Sprints are continuous and back-to-back — no calendar alignment, no waiting for the Product Owner, no gap after the Review.

text: True or False: An Increment must be released to customers or users at the end of each Sprint.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: False. A Done Increment must exist every Sprint, but it need not be released every Sprint — the Product Owner decides when to release based on value.

text: What is the accountability of the Product Owner during Sprint 0? (choose the best answer)
options: There is no such thing as Sprint 0.
Create the overall release plan to ensure that organizational goals are met.
Determine the composition of the Scrum Team to meet the release plan.
Gathering, eliciting and analyzing the requirements to build the Product Backlog.
Make sure enough Product backlog items are refined to fill the first 3 Sprints.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: there is no such thing as Sprint 0. Scrum has no special preparatory Sprint; every Sprint, including the first, produces a valuable Increment. The other options describe non-Scrum 'phase 0' activities.

text: True or False: When there are multiple teams working on one product, each Scrum Team should have a separate Product Owner.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. Multiple teams on one product share a single Product Owner (and one Product Backlog), keeping product direction coherent. A separate PO per team fragments ownership and priorities.

text: Which answer best describes the topics covered in Sprint Planning? (choose the best answer)
options: Who is the team and what team member roles will be.
What to do and who will do it.
What can be done, how to do it, and why to do it.
What went wrong in the last Sprint and what to do differently this Sprint.
How conditions have changed and how the Product Backlog should evolve.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: what can be done, how to do it, and why to do it. Sprint Planning answers the why (the Sprint Goal), the what (items selected from the Product Backlog), and the how (the plan). It is forward-looking; reviewing what went wrong belongs to the Retrospective.

text: Which of the following might the Scrum Team discuss during a Sprint Retrospective? (choose the best answer)
options: Methods of communication.
The way the Scrum Team does Sprint Planning.
Skills needed to improve the Scrum Teams ability to deliver.
The Definition of Done.
All of the above.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: all of the above. The Retrospective can cover communication methods, how the team runs its events, skills needed to improve delivery, and the Definition of Done — anything affecting the team's effectiveness.

text: An organization has decided to adopt Scrum, but management wants to change the terminology to fit with terminology already used. What will likely happen if this is done? (choose the best answer)
options: Without a new vocabulary as a reminder of the change, very little change may actually happen.
The organization may not understand what has changed with Scrum and the benefits of Scrum may be lost.
Management may feel less anxious.
All of the above.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: all of the above. Renaming Scrum terms to fit existing vocabulary tends to mask the change, so little actually changes, the organisation may miss what Scrum altered and lose its benefits, and management may simply feel more comfortable — none of which delivers the intended transformation.

text: Which three of the following are feedback loops in Scrum? (choose the best three answers)
options: Release Planning.
Refinement Meeting.
Sprint Retrospective.
Sprint Review.
Daily Scrum.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: Sprint Retrospective, Sprint Review, and Daily Scrum. These are the recurring inspect-and-adapt feedback loops. Release Planning and a separate Refinement Meeting are not defined Scrum events — refinement is an ongoing activity, not a loop.

text: The IT manager asks the Scrum Team for a status report describing the progress throughout the Sprint. The Scrum Team ask the Scrum Master for advice. The Scrum Master should: (choose the best answer)
options: Create and deliver the report to the manager herself.
Tell the Developers to figure it out themselves.
Tell the Developers to fit the report into the Sprint Backlog.
Talk to the IT manager and explain that the progress in Scrum comes from inspecting an Increment at the Sprint Review.
Ask the Product Owner to send the manager the report.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: talk to the IT manager and explain that in Scrum, progress is shown by inspecting a Done Increment at the Sprint Review. The Scrum Master coaches the organization toward transparency via real outcomes rather than producing side status reports or forcing them into the Sprint Backlog.

text: What happens if the Scrum Team cannot complete its work by the end of the Sprint? (choose the best answer)
options: The Sprint length is unchanged and the Scrum Team continuously learns and adapts.
The Sprint is extended temporarily. Lessons are taken to ensure it does not happen again.
The Sprint is extended and future Sprints use this new duration.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Sprint length is unchanged and the team keeps learning and adapting. Sprints are never extended to finish work; unfinished items return to the Product Backlog and the team improves. Extending the Sprint — once or permanently — breaks the timebox and empiricism.

text: User documentation is part of your Definition of Done. However, there are not enough Technical Writers for all teams. Your Scrum Team does not have a Technical Writer. What should the Scrum Team do? (choose the best answer)
options: Wait until you have a Technical Writer on your Scrum Team to take care of this.
Let the user documentation remain undone and accumulate until after the last development Sprint. It will then be done by any available Technical Writers.
The Developers on the Scrum Team should write the user documentation.
Form a separate team of Technical Writers that will work on an on-demand basis for the various Product Owners. Work order will be first in, first out.
trap: Done is defined by the Definition of Done, not by acceptance or partial completion.
explanation: Correct: the Developers on the team should write the user documentation. A cross-functional team does whatever is needed to meet its DoD, growing skills as required. Waiting for a specialist, deferring 'undone' documentation, or spinning up an on-demand writer pool all create hand-offs and undone work.

text: The Scrum Master observes the Product Owner is struggling with ordering the Product Backlog. What is an appropriate action for the Scrum Master to take? (choose the best answer)
options: Present the Product Owner with an ordered Product Backlog to use.
Suggest that the Developers order the Product Backlog to be sure that it is a feasible ordering of work.
Offer the Product Owner help in understanding that the goal of ordering the Product Backlog is to maximize value.
Encourage the Product Owner to work with the Developers to see which items technically are fastest to implement.
Suggest the Product Owner extend the Sprint, so he can have more time to order the Product Backlog.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: help the Product Owner understand that the goal of ordering is to maximize value. The Scrum Master coaches, they don't order the backlog themselves, delegate it to Developers, order by fastest-to-build, or extend the Sprint to buy time.

text: When must the Product Owner be present at the Daily Scrum? (choose the best answer)
options: When they need to represent the stakeholders' point of view.
When the Scrum Master asks them to attend.
When there are impediments to discuss.
When the Product Owner is actively working on items from the Sprint Backlog.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: when the Product Owner is actively working on Sprint Backlog items. The Daily is the Developers' event; the PO attends only if they're doing Sprint Backlog work — not to represent stakeholders, on the Scrum Master's request, or just because there are impediments.

text: How much of the Sprint Backlog must be defined during the Sprint Planning event? (choose the best answer)
options: Just enough to understand design and architectural implications.
Just enough tasks for the Scrum Master to be confident in the Developers' understanding of the Sprint.
The entire Sprint Backlog must be identified and estimated by the end of Sprint Planning.
Enough so the Developers can create their forecast of what work they can do.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: enough so the Developers can create their forecast of what work they can do. Only the near-term work needs planning; the Sprint Backlog is emergent and elaborated throughout the Sprint. Requiring the entire backlog to be estimated up front contradicts its emergent nature.

text: You are the Scrum Master of a new, to be developed Product. Development is going to require 45 people. What is a good first question for you to suggest the group thinks about when forming into teams? (choose the best answer)
options: What is the right mixture of senior and junior people on each team?
How will we make sure all teams have the right amount of expertise?
Who are the subject matter experts on each team?
Who are going to be the team leads?
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: how will we make sure all teams have the right amount of expertise? The key early concern is that each team is cross-functional enough to deliver value. Senior/junior mix, naming SMEs, or picking 'team leads' reflect traditional hierarchy, not self-managing cross-functional teams.

text: What activities would a Product Owner typically undertake in the period between the end of the current Sprint and the start of the next Sprint? (choose the best answer)
options: There are no such activities, the next Sprint starts immediately after the current Sprint.
Update the project plan with stakeholders.
Work with the Quality Assurance departments on the Increment of the current Sprint.
Refine the Product Backlog.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
