explanation: Correct: there are no such activities — the next Sprint starts immediately after the current one ends. There is no gap for plan updates, QA hand-offs, or a dedicated refinement slot; refinement is continuous within Sprints.

text: Several Sprints into a project, the Product Owner tells the Scrum Master that a key stakeholder just started using the product. The stakeholder is unhappy with the quality of the product. What are two good options for the Scrum Master? (choose the best two answers)
options: Explain to the Product Owner that it is up to the Developers to decide on acceptable quality standards.
Encourage the Product Owner to put quality specifications on the Product Backlog and express the stakeholder's concern to the Developers.
Coach the Product Owner on how to talk with the Developers about this concern.
Bring the concern to the Testers to improve how the Product is verified.
Wait to bring this up until the Sprint Retrospective.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: encourage the PO to put quality specifications on the Product Backlog and voice the concern to the Developers; and coach the PO on how to raise it with the Developers. Quality is addressed transparently and collaboratively with the team — not left solely to the Developers to define acceptable quality, routed through 'Testers', or deferred to the Retrospective.

text: As the Developers start work during the Sprint, they realize they have selected too much work to finish the Sprint. What should they do? (choose the best answer)
options: Inform the Product Owner at the Sprint review, but prior to the demonstration.
Find another Scrum Team to give the excess work to.
Reduce the Definition of Done and get all of the Product Backlog Items done by the new definition.
As soon as possible in the Sprint, work with the Product Owner to remove some work or Product Backlog Items.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: as soon as possible, work with the Product Owner to remove some work or items. Discovering overload is handled immediately by renegotiating scope with the PO while protecting the Sprint Goal — not by waiting for the Review, off-loading to another team, or lowering the DoD.

text: Who does the work to make sure Product Backlog Items conform to the Definition of Done? (choose the best answer)
options: The Quality Assurance Team.
The Scrum Master.
The Product Owner.
The Developers.
The Scrum Team.
trap: Done is defined by the Definition of Done, not by acceptance or partial completion.
explanation: Correct: the Developers. They do the work to make items conform to the DoD. It's not a separate QA team, the Scrum Master, the PO, or the whole Scrum Team collectively — the building work is the Developers'.

text: Which two things are appropriate for a Scrum Master to do if the Scrum Team does not have the tools and environment to completely finish each selected Product Backlog Item? (choose the best two answers)
options: Encourage the Product Owner to accept partially done Increments until the situation improves.
Have the Scrum Team establish a Definition of Done that is actually possible to achieve given current circumstances.
Declare the Scrum Team not ready for Scrum.
Refocus the current Sprint on establishing the Scrum Team's environment instead of delivering an Increment.
Coach the Scrum Team to improve its skills: tools and environment over time and adjust the Definition of Done accordingly.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: have the team set a DoD that is achievable given current circumstances, and coach the team to improve skills/tools/environment over time and adjust the DoD accordingly. Start with an honest DoD and raise the bar as capability grows — don't accept partial Increments, declare the team 'not ready', or spend the Sprint only on environment.

text: For the purpose of transparency, when does Scrum say a valuable and useful Increment must be available? (choose the best answer)
options: Every 3 Sprints.
When the Product Owner asks to create one.
After the Acceptance Testing phase.
At the end of every Sprint.
Before the Release Sprint.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: at the end of every Sprint. Every Sprint must yield at least one usable, valuable Increment so progress is transparent and inspectable — not every few Sprints, on demand, or only after a separate testing/release phase.

text: Who is accountable for clearly expressing Product Backlog Items? (choose the best answer)
options: The Product Owner.
The Business Analyst who represents the Product Owner.
The Scrum Master.
The Scrum Master, or the Scrum Master may have the Developers do it.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Product Owner. The PO is accountable for clearly expressing Product Backlog items so the team understands them — though others may help. It isn't a Business Analyst 'representing' the PO or the Scrum Master's task.

text: Which statement best describes the Sprint Review? (choose the best answer)
options: It is a mechanism to control the Developers activities during a Sprint.
It is used to congratulate the Developers if they complete their forecast or to punish the Developers if they fail to meet their forecast.
It is when the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the outcome of a Sprint and figure out what to do next.
It is a demo at the end of the Sprint for everyone in the organization to check on the work done
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: it is when the Scrum Team and stakeholders inspect the outcome of a Sprint and figure out what to do next. The Review is a collaborative working session about the product and its direction — not a control mechanism, a reward/punishment ceremony, or a passive demo.

text: Which three of the following are true about Scrum? (choose the best three answers)
options: Scrum is a framework for developing and sustaining complex products.
Scrum is a methodology where you can pick and choose which parts of Scrum you think will work for your environment.
Scrum implements self-management by replacing Project Managers with Scrum Masters.
Each component of Scrum serves a specific purpose and is essential to Scrum's success and your usage of Scrum to develop complex products.
Scrum is based on empiricism and lean thinking.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: Scrum is a framework for complex products; each component is essential and cannot be cherry-picked; and it is founded on empiricism and lean thinking. Scrum is not a pick-and-choose menu, and self-management is not achieved by simply swapping Project Managers for Scrum Masters.

text: As the Sprint Planning progresses, the Developers realize that the workload may be greater than their capacity to complete the work. Which two are valid actions? (choose the best two answers)
options: Recruit additional Developers before the work can begin.
The Developers ensure that the Scrum Team is aware, start the Sprint, and monitor progress.
The Developers work overtime during this Sprint.
Cancel the Sprint.
Remove or change selected Product Backlog Items.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Developers make the Scrum Team aware, start the Sprint, and monitor progress; and they remove or change selected items. Overload is handled by adjusting scope and inspecting as you go — not by recruiting mid-Sprint, working overtime, or cancelling the Sprint.

text: True or False: The Product Owner makes sure the Developers select enough from the Product Backlog for a Sprint to satisfy the stakeholders.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. The PO does not push the Developers to select 'enough' to satisfy stakeholders. The Developers decide how much they can forecast; forcing scope to please stakeholders undermines self-management and a realistic Sprint Goal.

text: The Daily Scrum is an event that happens every day. What would be three key concerns if the frequency were to be lowered to every two or three days? (choose the best three answers)
options: The Scrum Master loses the ability to update the Gantt Chart properly.
Too much work is spent updating the Scrum board before the meeting.
Opportunities to inspect and adapt the Sprint Backlog are lost.
The Product Owner cannot accurately report progress to the stakeholders.
Impediments are raised and resolved more slowly.
The Sprint Backlog may become inaccurate.
trap: The Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
explanation: Correct: opportunities to inspect and adapt the Sprint Backlog are lost, impediments are resolved more slowly, and the Sprint Backlog becomes inaccurate. Meeting less often lengthens the feedback loop and hides problems. The distractors invoke Gantt charts and PO status reporting — neither is a purpose of the Daily Scrum.

text: True or False: To get started in terms of what to build, Scrum requires no more than a Product Owner with enough ideas for a first Sprint, Developers to implement those ideas, and a Scrum Master to help guide the process.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: True. To start, Scrum needs little more than a Product Owner with enough of an idea for a first Sprint, Developers to build it, and a Scrum Master to guide the process. Scrum is deliberately lightweight; you don't need exhaustive upfront requirements.

text: How should a Scrum Team deal with non-functional requirements? (choose the best answer)
options: Make sure the release department understands these requirements, but it's not the Scrum Team's responsibility.
Manage them during the Integration Sprint prior to the Release Sprint.
Assign them to the Lead Developers on the team.
Ensure every Increment meets them.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: ensure every Increment meets the non-functional requirements. NFRs are satisfied continuously, built into every Increment (typically via the DoD). Handing them to a release department, an 'Integration Sprint', or lead developers pushes quality outside the Sprint.

text: At the end of a Sprint, a Product Backlog Item worked on during the Sprint does not meet the Definition of Done. What two things should happen with the undone Product Backlog Item? (choose the best two answers)
options: Do not include the item in the Increment this Sprint.
Put it on the Product Backlog for the Product Owner to decide what to do with it.
If the stakeholders agree, the Product Owner can accept it and release it to the users.
Review the item, add the done part of the estimate to the velocity and create a Story for the remaining work.
trap: Done is defined by the Definition of Done, not by acceptance or partial completion.
explanation: Correct: don't include the undone item in the Increment this Sprint, and put it back on the Product Backlog for the PO to decide. An item that misses the DoD simply isn't Done — you don't ship it on stakeholder say-so or count partial credit toward velocity.

text: Who should make sure everyone on the Scrum Team does their tasks for the Sprint? (choose the best answer)
options: The Project Manager.
The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master.
The Scrum Team.
All of the above.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Scrum Team. Self-management means the team collectively ensures the work gets done — no one person (PM, PO, or Scrum Master) polices individual task completion.

text: To create focus which of the following are most important to have ready when Sprint Planning begins? (choose the best two answers)
options: A fully refined Product Backlog.
A clear cadence of when the Daily Scrum will take place.
A Product Backlog with the most important items ready for discussion.
Formal budget approval to conduct another Sprint.
A Product Goal communicated by the Product Owner.
A clear and non-negotiable Sprint Goal.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: a Product Backlog with the most important items ready, and a Product Goal communicated by the Product Owner. These give Planning focus and direction. The backlog need not be fully refined, the Daily cadence is irrelevant to Planning, budget approval isn't a Scrum gate, and the Sprint Goal is an output of Planning, not a precondition.

text: True or False: A Product Owner is essentially the same thing as a traditional Project Manager?
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. A Product Owner is not a Project Manager. The PO maximizes product value and owns the Product Backlog; they don't direct, assign, or control the team like a traditional PM.

text: Which two statements explain why the Definition of Done is important to the Product Owner?
options: It identifies undone work that can be addressed in a separate Sprint.
It establishes the expected quality of the Increment reviewed at the Sprint Review.
It creates transparency regarding progress within the Scrum Team.
It helps the Product Owner track the open work during a Sprint.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: it establishes the expected quality of the Increment reviewed at the Sprint Review, and it creates transparency of progress within the team. For the Product Owner this means trustable, releasable quality and a clear view of what is truly Done — not a way to schedule 'undone' work into a later Sprint or to micro-track daily open tasks.

text: When does a Developer become accountable for the value of a Product Backlog Item selected for the Sprint? (choose the best answer)
options: Whenever a team member can accomodate more work.
At the Sprint Planning Event.
Never. The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating value every Sprint.
During the Daily Scrum.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: never — the entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating value every Sprint. Value accountability is collective, not pinned on an individual Developer at Planning or during the Daily Scrum.

text: True or False: A first Sprint can start before the Product Owner has a complete and exhaustive Product Backlog in place.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: True. A first Sprint can begin before an exhaustive Product Backlog exists — you need only enough to start, then refine continuously. Scrum is empirical, not big-design-up-front.

text: What is the Product Owner accountable for in Scrum?
options: Refining the top level Product Backlog Items until they are ready to be handed over to the Scrum Team.
Describing an Increment at Sprint Planning and making sure that the Developers deliver it by the end of the Sprint.
Writing the User Stories so they are comprehensive enough for the stakeholders.
Maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: maximizing the value of the product resulting from the Scrum Team's work. That is the PO's core accountability. It is not merely refining top items, describing/guaranteeing an Increment, or writing user stories for stakeholders.

text: The Product Owner's authority to change and update the Product Backlog is unlimited, except for:
options: High impact changes that have not been approved by the change request board.
Decisions by the chief program manager.
Decisions by the CFO, the CEO or the board of directors.
Technical and architectural work that needs to be done first, as indicated by the chief enterprise architect.
Items the Scrum Master has identified as impediments.
There are no exceptions, the entire organization must respect a Product Owner's decisions.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: there are no exceptions — the whole organization must respect the Product Owner's decisions. For the PO to be effective, their Product Backlog authority can't be overridden by boards, executives, architects, or the Scrum Master.

text: The Developers find out during the Sprint that they are not likely to build everything they forecast. What would you expect a Product Owner to do?
options: Cancel the Sprint.
Skip Product Backlog Refinement activities.
Change the Sprint Goal.
Re-negotiate the selected Product Backlog Items with the Developers.
Inform management that more resources are needed.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: re-negotiate the selected Product Backlog items with the Developers. Discovering the forecast won't fully land is handled by adjusting scope together while protecting the Sprint Goal — not cancelling the Sprint, changing the Goal, skipping refinement, or demanding more resources.

text: What should Developers do if the Product Owner is unavailable?
options: Wait until the Product Owner is available again.
Management should assign a substitue Product Owner to fill in where the Product Owner cannot be there.
Ask the Product Owner's manager to decide in the Product Owner's absence.
Within the Sprint, the Developers make the best decisions posssible to assure progress towards the Sprint Goal, re-aligning with the Product Owner once they are available again.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: within the Sprint, the Developers make the best decisions they can to progress toward the Sprint Goal, then re-align with the PO afterward. Self-managing teams keep moving during a PO's absence rather than stalling or having management parachute in a substitute.

text: What phrases best describe the relationship of the Product Owner and the Developers?
options: They should work apart as much as posssible in order to keep the concerns of business and technology separated.
They collaborate often so the Developers build Increments keeping end-user and stakeholder concerns in mind.
They collaborate often so the Product Owner can make informed decisions in balancing effort and value of Product Backlog Items.
They should share no more than the Sprint Planning and the Sprint Review meeting.
The Product Owner should be with the Developers full-time to grow a deep understanding of the technology being used.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: they collaborate often so Developers build with end-user/stakeholder concerns in mind, and so the PO can make informed effort-vs-value trade-offs. Close, frequent collaboration is the point — not working apart, limiting contact to two events, or the PO embedding full-time in the technology.

text: What is the principal value of releasing an Increment?
options: To learn about the Scrum Team's productivity.
To validate assumptions made when developing the product.
To learn about the forecast of functionality that was developed.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: to validate the assumptions made while developing the product. Releasing puts the product in front of real users to test whether the bet was right — it isn't primarily about measuring productivity or the functional forecast.

text: What best describes the relationship of the Product Owner and the stakeholders?
options: The Product Owner provides the stakeholders with acceptance forms at the Sprint Review to record their formal agreement over the delivered software.
The Product Owner actively asks for stakeholder input and expectations to incorporate into the Product Backlog.
The Product Owner has the final call over the requirements and should involve the stakeholders as little as possible.
The Product Owner rates the User Stories as provided by the stakeholders.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the PO actively seeks stakeholder input and expectations to incorporate into the Product Backlog. The relationship is collaborative and ongoing — not acceptance forms at the Review, minimizing stakeholder involvement, or merely rating stakeholder-written stories.

text: What are typical activities for a Product Owner in a Sprint?
options: Update the work plan for the Developers on a daily basis.
Create financial reporting upon the spent hours reported by the Scrum Team.
Work with the Developers on Product Backlog Refinement.
Attend every Daily Scrum to answer functional questions on the discussed Sprint Backlog items.
Collaborate with stakeholders, user communities, and subject matter experts.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: work with the Developers on Product Backlog refinement, and collaborate with stakeholders, user communities and SMEs. These are typical PO Sprint activities — not planning the Developers' daily work, producing hours-based financial reports, or attending every Daily.

text: Is the Product Owner required to be present at the Sprint Retrospective?
options: They are not allowed. The Sprint Retrosspective is an opportunity for the Developerss to improve.
They are optional. Attendance is only required when the Product Owner gets invited by the Scrum Master.
Their attendance is mandatory. The Sprint Retrospective is an opportunity for the Scrum Team to assess and improve itself.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: attendance is mandatory — the Retrospective is for the whole Scrum Team, including the PO, to inspect and improve itself. The PO is neither barred nor merely optional by invitation.

text: Adaptation requires regular inspection. In what ways does the Product Owner contribute to the results achieved by inspection?
options: The Product Owner invites stakeholders to the Sprint Review to learn how the current state of the marketplace influences what is the most valuable thing to do next.
The Product Owner verifies the Sprint Backlog for completeness at the end of Sprint Planning in order to allow the Sprint to start.
The Product Owner inspects the Sprint burn-down at the Daily Scrum for progress towards a complete Increment and re-planning the team's work.
The Product Owner shares the current state of Product Backlog at the Sprint Review, which, combined with the inspection of the Increment, leads to an updated Product Backlog.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the PO invites stakeholders to the Sprint Review to learn what is most valuable next, and shares the current Product Backlog at the Review so that, combined with inspecting the Increment, the backlog is updated. The PO does not gate Sprint Planning for 'completeness' or inspect a burn-down at the Daily Scrum — those overstep PO accountability.

text: Which description best fits the role of the Product Owner?
options: Chief Business Analyst.
Requirements Collector.
Project Manager 2.0.
Scope Protector.
Value Maximizer.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: Value Maximizer. That best captures the PO's essence. They are not a chief business analyst, requirements collector, project-manager-in-disguise, or scope protector.

text: Who creates the Definition of Done?
options: The Scrum Master as they are responsible for the Scrum Team's productivity.
The organization (or the Scrum Team if none is available from the organization).
The Product Owner as they are responsible for the product's success.
The Scrum Team, in a collaborative effort where the result is the common denominator of all members' definitions.
trap: Done is defined by the Definition of Done, not by acceptance or partial completion.
explanation: Correct: the organization provides it, or the Scrum Team creates it if the organization has no standard. The DoD may be an organisational standard that teams must at least meet; it isn't set solely by the Scrum Master or Product Owner, nor is it a lowest-common-denominator of individual opinions.

text: In order to make investment decisions, the Product Owner is likely to look at the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) of the product being built. What costs will a Product Owner take into account?
options: The accumulated cost over the earned value of the product.
The money spent on development and delivery of the product.
All investments required to conceive, develop, operate and maintain the product.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: all investments required to conceive, develop, operate and maintain the product. Total Cost of Ownership spans the whole life-cycle, not just development spend or an earned-value figure.

text: A Product Owner is entitled to postpone the start of a new Sprint after the conclusion of a previous Sprint for the following reason:
options: The Quality Assurance department needs more time to make the previous Increment complete.
The stakeholders are not happy with the value produced in the previous Sprint.
There is no acceptable reason. A new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint.
The Product Owner has not identified a Sprint Goal.
Not enough Product Backlog Items are ready.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: there is no acceptable reason — a new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one concludes. Sprints are continuous; you don't delay the next one for QA, unhappy stakeholders, a missing Sprint Goal, or unready items.

text: What two things best help the Product Owner manage the value of a product?
options: Devising a formula for a neutral calculation of value.
Setting value on individual Product Backlog Items using Value Poker.
The order of the Product Backlog.
Validating assumptions of value through frequent releases.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the order of the Product Backlog, and validating value assumptions through frequent releases. The PO manages value by ordering for value and testing assumptions in the market — not by inventing neutral value formulas or 'Value Poker' scores.

text: What is a Product Backlog?
options: It is a detailed lists of functionalities from which the Developers draw items, to be complemented by a separate Technology Backlog managed by the Developers.
The Product Backlog is an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product.
It is a list of references to Use Case documents that are stored in a central repository. The references should be visible and clickable by anybody to enhance transparency.
It is a formally approved list of requirements to be implemented over a set period.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product. That is the Scrum Guide's definition. It isn't split into a separate 'technology backlog', a set of document references, or a formally approved fixed requirements list.

text: To what extent does technical debt limit the value a Product Owner can get from a product?
options: Technical debt does not influence the delivery of value.
The velocity at which new functionality can be created is reduced when you have technical debt.
Technical debt causes a greater percentage of the product's budget to be spent on maintenance of the product.
Technical debt is not a Product Owner concern, technical debt is only an issue for the Developers.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: technical debt reduces the velocity at which new functionality can be created, and pushes a greater share of the budget into maintenance. Debt directly limits deliverable value and is very much a PO concern — not something only Developers worry about.

text: How does an organization know that a product built using Scrum is successful?
options: By the Product Owner and stakeholders accepting the Increment at the Sprint Review.
By releasing frequently, and measuring the value customers/users experience.
By measuring the actual time spent on development versus the time estimated for development.
By measuring the velocity has increased since the last release.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: by releasing frequently and measuring the value customers/users actually experience. Success is an outcome measured in the market, not internal acceptance at a Review, plan-vs-actual time, or rising velocity — velocity is a capacity signal, not value.

text: What is the main reason for the Product Owner to be part of the Daily Scrum?
options: It is not required for the Product Owner to participate.
To assign the Developers the daily tasks.
To track the progress of the Project.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: it is not required for the PO to participate in the Daily Scrum. It's the Developers' event; the PO doesn't attend to assign tasks or track project progress.

text: True or False: The Definition of Done increases the transparency and is used by the Developers to forecast how many items can be picked from the Product Backlog.
options: True.
False.
trap: Done is defined by the Definition of Done, not by acceptance or partial completion.
explanation: Correct: True. The Definition of Done makes the Increment's quality transparent, and because the Developers know what 'Done' entails, they can use it to forecast how many items they can realistically pull into a Sprint.

text: True or False: Sprint Planning is time-boxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: True. Sprint Planning is timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint, and usually shorter for shorter Sprints. As with all timeboxes it is an upper bound, not a required duration.

text: True or False: The Product Owner is the Scrum accountability that is responsible for engaging the product stakeholders.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: True. The Product Owner is the accountability responsible for engaging and representing the product's stakeholders and bringing their needs into the Product Backlog.

text: Which of the following topics can be part of the Sprint Retrospective?
options: Plan the next Sprint.
Discuss the way the Team has communicated in the last Sprint.
Discuss the way the Developers have collaborated with the Product Owner.
Refine Product Backlog Items.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: how the team has communicated, and how the Developers collaborated with the Product Owner. The Retrospective inspects people, interactions and process. Planning the next Sprint and refining Product Backlog items are separate activities, not Retrospective topics.

text: Which two statements are correct when four teams are working on one single product?
options: There can be only one Product Owner.
There can be only one Product Backlog.
There can be 4 Product Owners.
There can be 4 Product Backlogs.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: there can be only one Product Owner and only one Product Backlog. However many teams contribute to a single product, Scrum keeps one PO and one Backlog so direction stays coherent and transparent.

text: Who is the owner of the Product Backlog?
options: The Project Manager.
The whole Scrum Team.
The Scrum Master.
The Product Owner.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Product Owner. The PO owns and is accountable for the Product Backlog. Not the Project Manager (no such role), the whole Scrum Team, or the Scrum Master.

text: Which of the following are required by Scrum?
options: Hardening Sprints.
Story Points.
Time boxed events.
Sprint Planning meetings.
A Sprint 0.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: timeboxed events and Sprint Planning. Scrum requires its events (all timeboxed) including Sprint Planning. Hardening Sprints, Story Points, and a 'Sprint 0' are optional practices or non-Scrum add-ons, never requirements.

text: True or False: The Definition of Ready is defined by the Product Owner.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. A Definition of Ready is optional and, when used, is a team aid — it isn't 'defined by the Product Owner'. (The DoD, which is required, is owned by the whole team.)

text: True or False: The Sprint Review is considered as a "formal meeting".
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: False. The Sprint Review is explicitly an informal working session to inspect the Increment and collaborate on next steps — the Scrum Guide describes it as a working session, not a formal meeting or sign-off gate.

text: Please select the answer representing a responsibility of a Product Owner.
options: Ordering the items in the Product Backlog to best achieve goals and missions.
Defining the Definition of Done.
Defining the Definition of Ready.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: ordering the Product Backlog to best achieve goals and mission. That's a PO responsibility. Defining the Definition of Done is the whole team's, and a Definition of Ready is optional — neither is a PO-owned responsibility.

text: Which of the following should not be changed during a Sprint?
options: Product Backlog.
Definition of Done.
The Sprint Backlog.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Definition of Done. The DoD should stay stable within a Sprint (changing it mid-Sprint would move the goalposts on quality). By contrast the Product Backlog and Sprint Backlog are living artifacts that evolve during the Sprint.

text: Which of the following is a Scrum Value?
options: Creativity.
Inspection.
Adaption.
Focus.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: Focus. The five Scrum Values are commitment, focus, openness, respect, and courage. 'Creativity' isn't one, and inspection/adaptation are empirical pillars, not values.

text: Which statement is not correct about the Scrum Daily?
options: It is moderated by the Product Owner.
The Developers have to participate in the meeting.
It is a time boxed event (15 min).
It should be held at the same time and place.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct (the incorrect statement): 'It is moderated by the Product Owner.' The Daily Scrum is run by and for the Developers; the PO does not moderate it. The other statements are true — Developers participate, it is timeboxed to 15 minutes, and it is held at the same time and place each day to reduce complexity.

text: Which questions does the Sprint Planning answer?
options: What can be delivered in the Increment resulting from the upcoming Sprint?
Who will do which Sprint Backlog item?
How will the work needed to deliver the Increment be achieved?
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: what can be delivered in the Increment, and how the work will be achieved. Planning answers the what and the how (plus the why, the Sprint Goal). Who does which specific item is decided by the Developers as they self-manage — it is not fixed in Planning.

text: True or False: More Velocity means more Value!
options: True.
False.
trap: Velocity is not a measure of product value or cross-team performance.
explanation: Correct: False. More velocity does not mean more value — velocity measures output/capacity, while value is about the outcomes delivered to users and the business.

text: Which two of the following are not correct about non-functional requirements?
options: The Project Manager takes care of non-functional requirements.
Non-functional requirements can be added to the Product Backlog.
Non-functional requirements are reflected in the Sprint Goal.
Non-functional requirements can be added to the Definition of Done.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct (the two incorrect statements): 'the Project Manager takes care of non-functional requirements' and 'NFRs are reflected in the Sprint Goal.' There is no Project Manager in Scrum, and NFRs aren't captured in the Sprint Goal. The valid homes for NFRs are the Product Backlog and, when they must hold every Sprint, the Definition of Done.

text: What should the Product Owner do when the Developers are ready to start the first Sprint, but the Product Backlog is not ready yet?
options: The Product Owner should ask the Scrum Master to remove this impediment.
The Product Owner should let the team start the Sprint and continue refining the Product Backlog.
The Product Owner should not allow the team to Start the Sprint.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the PO should let the team start the Sprint and keep refining the Product Backlog. You don't need a 'ready' backlog to begin — refinement is continuous. Blocking the Sprint or treating an unfinished backlog as an impediment misunderstands Scrum's emergent nature.

text: True or False: The Definition of Done shouldn't be changed in the middle of the Sprint.
options: True.
False.
trap: Done is defined by the Definition of Done, not by acceptance or partial completion.
explanation: Correct: True. The Definition of Done should not change mid-Sprint, as that would alter what 'Done' means partway through and break transparency of the Increment. It can be revisited between Sprints, typically at the Retrospective.

text: What is the perfect number of hours a Developer should work in a week?
options: As long as it is needed.
A maximum of 40 hours per week.
It is required to work at a constant pace.
Between 40 and 60 hours per week.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: it is required to work at a constant, sustainable pace. Scrum sets no 'perfect' or maximum weekly hours; it asks teams to sustain a pace they can maintain indefinitely, which supports quality and predictability.

text: Which of the following answers can be reasons for the Scrum Master to attend the Daily Scrum?
options: To be able to track the Sprint progress.
It is not necessary for the Scrum Master to attend the meeting.
To support the Product Owner.
The Developers have asked the Scrum Master to facilitate the Daily Scrum.
trap: The Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
explanation: Correct: it is not necessary for the Scrum Master to attend, and they may attend if the Developers ask them to facilitate. The Daily is the Developers' event; the Scrum Master isn't there to track progress or support the PO.

text: What is the main role of a QA in Scrum?
options: Support to have less technical debt.
Support the Testers in the process.
There are no QA's in Scrum.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: there are no QAs in Scrum. Everyone who builds the Increment is a 'Developer', and quality is a whole-team responsibility — there is no separate QA accountability.

text: True or False: The Sprint Backlog content is emerging during the Sprint.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: True. The Sprint Backlog is emergent — the Developers add and refine work throughout the Sprint as more is learned about what's needed to meet the Sprint Goal.

text: How many Developers are in a Scrum Team?
options: 1 to 9.
3 to 9.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: 3 to 9 Developers. The 2020 guide describes a Scrum Team of typically 10 or fewer people; commonly framed as 3–9 Developers plus the PO and Scrum Master. Smaller teams risk skill gaps; larger ones add coordination overhead.

text: True or False: When n Scrum teams are working on a product, there should always be only 1 Product Owner but 1-n Scrum Masters.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: True. With n teams on one product there is always exactly one Product Owner, but there can be one or more Scrum Masters (a Scrum Master may serve several teams, or each team may have its own).

text: What is the main accountability of a Project Manager in Scrum?
options: Supporting the Product Owner.
Tracking the progress of a Release.
There are no Project Managers in Scrum.
Managing Risks.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: there are no Project Managers in Scrum. Scrum distributes traditional PM responsibilities across the three accountabilities rather than having a PM role.

text: What does a burn-down chart measure in a project?
options: Work remaining across time.
Business value delivered by the team.
Budget remaining across time.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: work remaining across time. A burn-down chart plots how much work is left as the Sprint (or release) progresses. It does not measure business value delivered or budget — those are different concerns.

text: What may happen if the Scrum Teams composition changes during the project?
options: The productivity will increase due to new ideas.
The roles are clearly defined – nothing will happen.
Often a short-term reduction in productivity can be seen.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: often a short-term reduction in productivity. Changing team composition disrupts the team's rhythm and shared understanding, so productivity typically dips before recovering — it doesn't simply rise or stay flat.

text: Which statement explain when a Product Backlog Item is considered "Done"?
options: When the Product Owner declares it to be "Done".
When the Developers agrees that it is "Done".
When it is potentially releasable.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: when it is potentially releasable. An item is Done when it meets the Definition of Done and is in a usable, releasable state — not merely when the PO or Developers 'declare' it done by opinion.

text: How should the Developers react, when they realize that they have overcommitted themselves in a Sprint?
options: They should collaborate with the Product Owner and decide together how to adjust the Sprint Backlog.
They should ask the Scrum Master to cancel the Sprint.
They should keep this information to themselves until the next Sprint Review.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: collaborate with the Product Owner and decide together how to adjust the Sprint Backlog. Overcommitment is resolved by renegotiating scope with the PO while protecting the Sprint Goal — not by cancelling the Sprint or hiding it until the Review.

text: Which statements about the Product Backlog are correct?
options: The Product Backlog contains only items that are completely refined.
In the Product Backlog, Items at the top are usually smaller than on the bottom.
The Product Backlog is never baselined.
The Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: top items are usually smaller than lower ones; the Product Backlog is never baselined; and the Product Owner is accountable for it. Higher-ordered items are more refined and smaller. It does not contain only fully-refined items — lower items stay coarse.

text: Which of the following statements are correct about "technical debt"?
options: If you have a high level of "technical debt", it could lead to false assumptions about the current state of the system.
If you have "technical debt", no further features should be developed until the "technical debt" is fixed.
It creates uncertainty, because when you add more and more features more and more problems will occur.
It is the task of the Product Owner to take it into account during the release planning.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: high technical debt can create false assumptions about the system's true state, and it adds uncertainty because each new feature can surface more problems. It is not a rule that all feature work stops until debt is cleared, nor is managing debt a Product Owner release-planning task — quality is the whole team's concern via the DoD.

text: The Developers have some trouble to understand a Sprint Backlog item – what should they do?
options: Ask the Scrum Master to explain it to them.
Don't touch the item until the Sprint Review to discuss it with the Product Owner again.
Collaborate with the Product Owner immediately to receive a better understanding.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: collaborate with the Product Owner immediately for a better understanding. Ambiguity is resolved right away through conversation — not by asking the Scrum Master to interpret requirements or parking the item until the Review.

text: What kind of testing should be done during the Sprint?
options: Test Driven Development.
Acceptance Tests.
Unit Tests.
All kind of test required to create a working Increment.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: all kinds of testing required to create a working Increment. Whatever testing is needed to reach 'Done' happens inside the Sprint — there is no deferring tests to a later phase. Naming one technique (TDD, unit, acceptance) alone is too narrow.

text: Which two statements about the Developers are correct?
options: The Developers are self-managing.
The Developers are not allowed to help the Product Owner managing the Product Backlog.
The Developers decide when to do the next release.
The Developers own the Definition of Done.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Developers are self-managing, and the Developers own the Definition of Done. They organize their own work and are accountable for the quality standard. They may help the PO with the backlog, and they don't decide releases (that's the PO's call).

text: Which Scrum accountability is responsible to do all the work required to turn Product Backlog in potentially releasable items?
options: The Business Analyst.
The Project Manager.
The Developers.
The Stakeholders.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Developers. They do all the work to turn Product Backlog items into potentially releasable Increments. Not a Business Analyst, Project Manager, or stakeholders.

text: True or False: The Product Owner has to maximize the value – more features always bring more value. Therefore, the Product Owner has to maximize the number of features in a Sprint.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. More features do not always mean more value — often the opposite (added cost, complexity, unused functionality). The PO maximizes value, which frequently means building less, not more.

text: Yes or No: The Product Owner can ask a developer to order the Product Backlog Items instead of him/her – is that okay?
options: Yes.
No.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: yes. The Product Owner remains accountable for ordering but may delegate the actual ordering work to others, including a Developer — accountability stays with the PO even when the work is delegated.

text: Which accountability in Scrum is responsible for explaining the items of the Product Backlog?
options: The Developer.
The Requirements Engineer.
The Project Manager.
The Scrum Master.
The Product Owner.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Product Owner. The PO is accountable for clearly expressing and explaining Product Backlog items. Not a Requirements Engineer, Project Manager, Scrum Master, or an individual Developer.

text: Which two of the following services are expected from a Scrum Master to a Product Owner?
options: The Scrum Master should help the Product Owner to find techniques for managing the Product Backlog.
The Scrum Master should help the Product Owner to do the documentation.
The Scrum Master should remove impediments for the Scrum Team (incl. Product Owner).
The Scrum Master should act as a "middleman" between the Product Owner and the Developers.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: help the PO find techniques for managing the Product Backlog, and remove impediments for the Scrum Team (including the PO). The Scrum Master serves the PO by coaching and clearing obstacles — not by doing their documentation or acting as a go-between with the Developers.

text: True or False: Only the Developers are influencing the Definition of Done, no one else.
options: True.
False.
trap: Done is defined by the Definition of Done, not by acceptance or partial completion.
explanation: Correct: False. While the Developers must be able to meet the DoD, they are not the only influence — if the organisation has a standard, the team must at least conform to it, and the DoD is shaped collaboratively to serve transparency and quality.

text: Which of the following are benefits of self-managing teams?
options: Increase of predictability.
Increase of respect.
Increase of individual buy-in.
Increase of creativity.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: increased individual buy-in and increased creativity. Owning their decisions makes people more invested and inventive. Predictability and 'respect' aren't the defining benefits of self-management here.

text: When can a Sprint be cancelled?
options: When the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete.
When the Developers are asking the Product Owner to do it.
When the Business Analyst is asking the Product Owner to do it.
When the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete and no items are "Done" yet.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint, and the trigger is an obsolete Sprint Goal — regardless of how many items are already Done. A request from Developers or a Business Analyst is not itself a reason.

text: If the Product Owner has concerns about the Definition of Done (DoD) – what should the Product Owner do?
options: The Product Owner should discuss the Definition of Done with the Developers.
The Product Owner should change the Definition of Done.
The Product Owner should ask the Scrum Master to change the Definition of Done.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the Product Owner should discuss the Definition of Done with the Developers. The DoD is owned collaboratively; the PO raises concerns and collaborates rather than unilaterally changing it or ordering the Scrum Master to change it.

text: Which of the following are not required by Scrum?
options: Using User Stories.
Have a Product Owner.
Answering the "three questions" in the Daily Scrums.
Having time boxed Scrum Events.
Have a Sprint Backlog.
Using the concept of Story Points.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct (not required by Scrum): User Stories, the 'three questions' at the Daily Scrum, and Story Points. These are popular optional practices. Scrum does require a Product Owner and a Sprint Backlog, and its events must be timeboxed.

text: What does it mean for a team to be a "cross-functional" Team?
options: The team should be able to collaborate with different departments.
Each of the team members should be a developer, Tester and architect.
The team has all the expertise (not each person) required to transform a Product Backlog Item in a potentially releasable Increment.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the team collectively has all the expertise (not each person) to turn a Product Backlog item into a releasable Increment. Cross-functional is a team-level property — it doesn't require every individual to be developer+tester+architect, nor is it merely 'collaborating with other departments'.

text: Which two of the following answers are not correct about the Product Owner accountability?
options: The Product Owner decides which developer does what.
The Product Owner has to participate in the Daily Scrum.
The Product Owner measures the progress of a release.
The Product Owner is responsible for maximizing the value.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct (the two incorrect statements): 'the PO decides which Developer does what' and 'the PO has to participate in the Daily Scrum'. Neither is true — Developers self-assign work, and the PO isn't required at the Daily. Maximizing value and tracking release progress are legitimate PO concerns.

text: True or False: Scrum can only be used to develop products, not to maintain/sustain existing ones.
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: False. Scrum can be used to develop and to sustain/maintain products — the Scrum Guide explicitly covers developing and sustaining complex products.

text: What can be done to reduce technical debt?
options: Improve the Definition of Done.
Include external QA.
Have hardening Sprints.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: improve the Definition of Done. Strengthening the DoD raises the quality bar every Sprint, which prevents debt from accumulating. External QA and hardening Sprints push quality outside the Sprint, which Scrum avoids.

text: True or False: The Scrum Master can decide which Scrum Events are required in the Scrum project.
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: False. The Scrum Master cannot pick which events are 'required' — all Scrum events are mandatory. The Scrum Master ensures Scrum is understood and enacted, not selectively applied.

text: Which of the following is not a feedback loop in Scrum?
options: The Sprint Review.
The Sprint Planning.
The Product Backlog Grooming.
The Daily Scrum.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct (not a feedback loop): Product Backlog Grooming. Refinement is an ongoing activity, not an inspect-and-adapt event. The Sprint Review, Sprint Planning and Daily Scrum are all feedback loops.

text: True or False: When n Scrum teams are working on a product, there are n Sprint Backlogs but only 1 Product Backlog.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: True. With n teams on one product there are n Sprint Backlogs (one per team) but a single shared Product Backlog for the product.

text: True or False: Sprint Review is not a formal meeting.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: True. The Sprint Review is an informal working session, not a formal meeting — its purpose is collaborative inspection of the Increment and adaptation of the Product Backlog.

text: When is it allowed for a Scrum Master to cancel a Sprint?
options: When the Sprint Goal is obsolete.
When the Developers ask the Scrum Master to do so.
The Scrum Master does not have the authority to do this.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Scrum Master does not have the authority to cancel a Sprint. Only the Product Owner can cancel a Sprint, and only when the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete — not on a Scrum Master's or Developers' request.

text: What happens usually between a Sprint Retrospective and the next Sprint Planning?
options: User Story "grooming".
Nothing!
Product Backlog Refinement.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: nothing. Sprints are continuous, so there is no defined activity or gap between the Retrospective and the next Sprint Planning — the next Sprint simply begins. Refinement happens within Sprints, not in a between-Sprint slot.

text: True or False: When 3 products are developed using Scrum, there can be only a single Product Owner for all products.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. Each product has its own Product Owner; three products would normally have three POs (though one person could hold more than one PO accountability, there isn't a rule forcing 'a single PO for all'). The framing as a required single PO across products is wrong.

text: Which of the following is correct about the Product Vision?
options: It is an old concept and overall not recommended.
It helps the Product Owner to decide when the product is releasable.
It gives an overall direction to all Sprints, makes it easier to prioritize Product Backlog Items and helps the team to stay focused.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Product Vision gives overall direction to all Sprints, makes prioritizing items easier, and helps the team stay focused. It's a valuable, current concept — not outdated, and not merely a releasability signal.

text: Which statement describes best how the Product Backlog is impacted by changes in the product environment?
options: The Product Backlog should always follow the Product Owners plan and should not reflect the changes at all.
The Product Backlog should be very high level and therefore tolerate such changes.
The Product Backlog should evolve and reflect the environment changes.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Product Backlog should evolve and reflect environment changes. It is a living artifact that adapts as the market, technology, and understanding shift — it neither ignores change nor stays deliberately vague to 'absorb' it.

text: What does a Product Owner do in the Scrum Event Sprint Retrospective?
options: Answering the questions of the Developers and Scrum Master.
The Product Owner does not have the permission to attend the meeting.
Participate as a Scrum Team member.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: participate as a Scrum Team member. In the Retrospective the PO takes part like any other member to help the team inspect and improve — they're neither barred nor merely there to answer questions.

text: Which of the following are not allowed in Scrum?
options: Using User Stories.
Having two Product Owners in a Scrum Team.
A Sprint 0.
A Release Sprint.
Using Story Points.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct (not allowed): having two Product Owners in a Scrum Team, a 'Sprint 0', and a 'Release Sprint'. Scrum mandates exactly one Product Owner and continuous, uniform Sprints. User Stories and Story Points are optional but permitted.

text: True or False: When two Scrum Teams are working on the same product you should normalize their estimations to be able to compare their performance.
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: False. You should not normalize estimates to compare teams' performance. Estimates are a team-internal aid, not a cross-team performance metric — comparing velocities pits teams against each other and misuses the numbers.

text: Which statement about the Product Backlog is correct?
options: The Product Backlog must only contain small, detailed and clearly described items.
The Scrum Master is responsible for managing the Product Backlog.
The Product Owner is responsible for managing the Product Backlog.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Product Owner is responsible for managing the Product Backlog. It need not contain only small, detailed items (lower items stay coarse), and the Scrum Master does not manage it.

text: True or False: The Product Owner can nominate a "Lead Developer" as a single point of contact.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. The PO cannot nominate a 'Lead Developer' as a single point of contact — Developers are self-managing with no hierarchy, and the PO collaborates with all of them.

text: Which 3 of the following are time boxed Scrum events?
options: Sprint Planning.
Sprint Refinement.
Sprint Review.
Daily Scrum.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: Sprint Planning, Sprint Review, and Daily Scrum are timeboxed events. 'Sprint Refinement' is not a Scrum event — refinement is an ongoing activity.

text: Which of the following answers is correct about the Product Owner accountability?
options: The Product Owner is not part of the Scrum Team.
The Product Owner creates all items in the Product Backlog on his own.
The Product Owner is responsible to explain Product Backlog Items and to answer questions.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the PO is responsible for explaining Product Backlog items and answering questions about them. The PO IS part of the Scrum Team and need not personally author every item alone.

text: Which statement is correct about the Sprint Backlog?
options: It doesn't need to have detail.
It has just enough detail.
It has all the details.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: it has just enough detail. The Sprint Backlog needs enough detail for the Developers to inspect progress at the Daily Scrum and self-manage — not zero detail, and not exhaustive up-front detail, since it emerges through the Sprint.

text: How much of the overall working time should the Product Owner spend with the Developers?
options: At least 15% of the time.
As much as required.
Min. 50% of the time.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: as much as required. Time with the Developers is driven by need and value assurance, not a fixed 15% or 50% quota.

text: True or False: Two Scrum Teams are working on the same product. Do they have to share the same Definition of Ready?
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: False. Two teams on the same product do not have to share a Definition of Ready — 'Ready' is an optional, team-chosen aid. (They must, however, share a Definition of Done to produce a common Increment.)

text: Based on which criteria should the Product Owner order the Product Backlog Items?
options: Based on size.
Based on value.
Based on risk.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: based on value. The primary ordering driver is value toward the Product Goal, with risk, dependencies and size as further inputs — but value leads. Ordering purely by size or risk alone misses the point.

text: The satisfaction of which stakeholder is the most important?
options: The CEO.
The higher management.
The End-user.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the end-user. Ultimately the product must deliver value to those who use it; user satisfaction outweighs pleasing the CEO or higher management as the measure of a valuable product.

text: True or False: It is not allowed that the Product Owner is a Developer (part of the "Developers") at the same time.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. It is allowed for the Product Owner to also be one of the Developers — Scrum doesn't forbid one person holding the PO accountability and doing development work, though it can be challenging.

text: Which 2 of the following are an indication for an item to be ready for development?
options: The item is refined and small enough to fit in one Sprint.
All stakeholder have agreed to prioritize it.
The item is estimated (e.g. in Story Points).
The item is smaller than 15 Story Points.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the item is refined and small enough to fit in one Sprint, and it is estimated. 'Ready' items are understood, sized and small enough to complete in a Sprint. Universal stakeholder sign-off and a fixed point ceiling are not Scrum criteria.

text: True or False: To be self-management means, that it is okay for the Developers to don't do the Daily Scrum.
options: True.
False.
trap: The Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
explanation: Correct: False. Self-management does not permit skipping the Daily Scrum — all Scrum events are required. Teams choose how to run the Daily, not whether to hold it.

text: The Product Owner is not available and cannot answer the developers questions before the Sprint Planning. Therefore, the developers feel a high level of uncertainty to make a reliable forecast. What should the team do?
options: Extend the duration of the current Sprint and try to answer all questions.
The Sprint Planning meeting should be cancelled or postponed.
The upcoming Sprint should be cancelled.
The developers should make a best guess and should not worry too much.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: the Developers should make a best guess and not worry too much. With an unavailable PO, the team makes a reasonable forecast and adapts as understanding improves — Scrum is empirical. Extending or cancelling Sprints/Planning over uncertainty is an overreaction.

text: Which of the following should a Scrum Master do to start a project?
options: Ask the Lead Developer to explain the IT architecture.
Ask the Developers to introduce themselves to each other and tell about their skills and background.
Ensure, that all team members have a first ticket assigned to them.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: ask the Developers to introduce themselves and share their skills and background. A Scrum Master starts by helping the team form and understand its collective capabilities — not by having a lead explain the architecture or pre-assigning tickets.

text: True or False: All items in the Product Backlog have usually the same size.
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: False. Product Backlog items are usually not the same size — higher-ordered items are refined smaller, while lower items remain larger and coarser.

text: Which two of the following are typical Daily Scrum outcomes?
options: The team is clear on the next steps toward the Sprint Goal.
The tasks are assigned to the developer.
Impediments identified by the Scrum Master.
A refined Daily Backlog.
trap: The Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
explanation: Correct: the team is clear on next steps toward the Sprint Goal, and impediments are surfaced. The Daily produces an updated plan and visible blockers — it does not assign tasks to individuals or produce a 'refined Daily Backlog'.

text: True or False: Does a Product Backlog Item have an item "Owner".
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: False. Product Backlog items don't have individual 'owners'. The Product Owner is accountable for the whole backlog, and the Developers collectively own the work — assigning per-item owners contradicts self-management.

text: True or False: The Product Owner is not part of the Scrum Team.
options: True.
False.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: False. The Product Owner IS part of the Scrum Team, alongside the Developers and Scrum Master. There are no separate 'sub-teams'.

text: Which statements describe best what happens in an organization if Scrum is introduced but the Scrum terminology is tailored to fit into the organizations environment?
options: The change might be not obvious to everyone and therefore little change will happen.
The organization will adapt the Scrum concepts faster due to the tailored approach.
The management may feel less enthusiastic about the new approach.
The change might not be obvious to every employee and some employees will not recognize it at all.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the change may not be obvious so little changes; management may be less enthusiastic; and some employees may not recognise the change at all. Renaming Scrum to fit existing terms tends to hide the shift rather than accelerate adoption.

text: Which Scrum accountabilities have to attend the Daily Scrum?
options: The Scrum Master.
The Project Manager.
The Developers.
The Product Owner.
The Business Analyst.
trap: The Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
explanation: Correct: the Developers. The Daily Scrum is by and for the Developers, so they are the ones required to attend. The Scrum Master and Product Owner attend only if actively working on Sprint Backlog items; there is no Project Manager or Business Analyst role in Scrum.

text: The Developers have an internal conflict with one of the team members. What should the Product Owner do?
options: Remove the Developer from the team?
Ask the Scrum Master to remove the Developer from the Team?
Let the team handle the conflict internally – they are self-managing!
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: let the team handle the conflict internally — they are self-managing. Interpersonal issues are resolved by the self-managing team. It is not the PO's role to remove a Developer or to have the Scrum Master do so.

text: Which of the following describes best the Sprint Review?
options: It is a meeting for the inspection of the Increment and to collect feedback.
It is a meeting to do the controlling and evaluation in regards to the developers work.
It is a formal meeting to receive the approval for the work that was done.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: it is a meeting to inspect the Increment and collect feedback. The Sprint Review is collaborative inspection and adaptation of the product, not a control/evaluation session or a formal approval gate for the Developers' work.

text: True or False: In each Sprint Backlog at least one high priority process improvement items is existing.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: False. Scrum does not mandate that every Sprint Backlog contains a process-improvement item. (That was a 2017-guide suggestion; the 2020 Scrum Guide does not require it.)

text: True or False: The Definition of Ready shows the team when Product Backlog Items are ready to be selected for the Sprint Backlog.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: False. A Definition of Ready is an optional practice; Scrum does not define or require it. (The Definition of Done, by contrast, is required.)

text: Which two of the following contribute the most to the Scrum Value "Focus"?
options: Having a Burn-Down-Chart.
Having a Sprint Goal.
Using Story Points.
Having time boxed events.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: having a Sprint Goal, and having timeboxed events. Both create focus — a single objective to rally around and bounded time to concentrate effort. Burn-downs and Story Points are optional tools, not drivers of the Focus value.

text: Who is required to attend the Daily Scrum?
options: The Product Owner.
The Project Lead.
The Developers.
The Scrum Master
trap: The Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
explanation: Correct: the Developers. The Daily Scrum is the Developers' event, so they are required. The Product Owner and Scrum Master participate only if they are working on Sprint Backlog items.

text: How much time is needed between a Sprint Retrospective and the next Sprint Planning to prepare the Product Backlog?
options: As much as defined by the Scrum Master.
As much as it is needed.
None.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: none. Sprints are continuous — no time is reserved between the Retrospective and the next Planning to prepare the backlog. Product Backlog refinement is ongoing within Sprints.

text: Which of the following best describes the Scrum Pillar "Transparency"?
options: The whole process should be visible to everyone.
The process should be visible to the key stakeholders.
Significant aspect of the process must be visible to those responsible for the outcome.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: significant aspects of the process must be visible to those responsible for the outcome. Transparency is targeted at the people who make decisions from the artifacts — it doesn't require exposing everything to everyone, only what matters for sound inspection.

text: True or False: The Product Backlog is baselined before the Sprint 0.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: False. The Product Backlog is never baselined or frozen, and there is no 'Sprint 0' in Scrum — the backlog emerges and evolves continuously.

text: Which of the following are Scrum Values?
options: Respect.
Focus.
Inspection.
Collaboration.
Commitment.
Maximize Value.
Courage.
Openness.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: Respect, Focus, Commitment, Courage, Openness — the five Scrum Values. 'Inspection' and 'Collaboration' aren't values (inspection is an empirical pillar), and 'Maximize Value' is a PO goal, not a value.

text: True or False: Self-management means, that the team can decide which Scrum events are needed.
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: False. Self-management does not let a team decide which Scrum events are needed — all events are required. Teams decide how to carry them out, not whether to hold them.

text: True or False: Following Scrum, there can be a maximum of one release per Sprint.
options: True.
False.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: False. There is no maximum of one release per Sprint — a team can release multiple times within a Sprint (or continuously). The PO decides release timing based on value.

text: Which Scrum accountability is owning the Sprint Backlog?
options: The Product Owner.
The Scrum Master
The Developers.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Developers. The Sprint Backlog is owned by the Developers, who create and manage it to meet the Sprint Goal. The Product Owner owns the Product Backlog; the Scrum Master owns none of the artifacts.

text: Which of the following are mandatory in Scrum?
options: Do Sprint Plannings.
Do Daily Scrums.
Have a Product Owner.
Use Story Points.
Use User Stories.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: doing Sprint Plannings, doing Daily Scrums, and having a Product Owner. These are mandatory in Scrum. Story Points and User Stories are optional practices, not requirements.

text: True or False: The Scrum Master can decide which Scrum Artifacts are required in the Scrum project.
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: False. The Scrum Master cannot choose which artifacts are 'required' — the three artifacts (Product Backlog, Sprint Backlog, Increment) are all mandatory.

text: How is budgeting done in a Scrum Project?
options: Ideally budgeting is done every Sprint.
Scrum doesn't need the team to care about budget.
