Budgeting is done based on the Product Backlog as a baseline.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: ideally budgeting is done every Sprint. Scrum's empirical, incremental approach lends itself to funding decisions revisited each Sprint based on demonstrated value — rather than a single upfront budget baselined against the whole backlog.

text: The collaboration between the Developers and the Product Owner is very important for the product. Which of the following is the least productive way for the Scrum Master to improve this collaboration?
options: The Scrum Master should act as a go-between for them.
The Scrum Master should teach them techniques to improve it.
The Scrum Master should suggest new collaboration tools.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct (least productive): the Scrum Master acting as a go-between for the Developers and Product Owner. Relaying messages keeps them apart and weakens collaboration. Teaching them collaboration techniques or suggesting better tools helps them work together directly, which is the goal.

text: Which Scrum Event can be compared to the use of a "lessons learned meeting"?
options: The Sprint Review.
The Daily Scrum.
The Sprint Retrospective.
The Sprint Planning.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Sprint Retrospective. Like a 'lessons learned' session, the Retrospective inspects how the last Sprint went and plans improvements — but it happens every Sprint, not just at project end.

text: True or False: The Product Backlog should have just enough detail.
options: True.
False.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: True. The Product Backlog should have just enough detail — more refinement near the top for near-term work, less further down. Over-detailing everything up front wastes effort on items that may change.

text: In the middle of the Sprint, the customer decides that there are two new features she wants. The Product Owner could: (choose the best two answers)
options: Ask the Developers to consider whether they can add these features to the current Sprint without endangering the Sprint Goal.
Introduce these features at the next Daily Scrum.
Have the Scrum Master add these features to the current Sprint.
Add these features to the Product Backlog.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: ask the Developers whether they can add the features without endangering the Sprint Goal, and add the features to the Product Backlog. New requests are weighed against the Sprint Goal and normally flow through the backlog — not forced in via the Scrum Master or simply announced at the Daily.

text: Developers are self-managing, which of the following do they manage? (choose the best answer)
options: Product Backlog ordering.
When to release, based on its progress.
Sprint Backlog.
Stakeholders for the Sprint Review.
Sprint length.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Sprint Backlog. Self-managing Developers own the Sprint Backlog and how they do the work. They don't control Product Backlog ordering, release decisions, Review stakeholders, or Sprint length — those sit elsewhere.

text: When the Developers determine that they will not be able to finish the complete forecast, who needs to be present when reviewing and adjusting the Sprint work selected? (choose the best answer)
options: The Scrum Master and the Developers.
The Product Owner and all stakeholders.
The Product Owner and the Developers.
The Scrum Master project manager and the Developers.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Product Owner and the Developers. Renegotiating Sprint scope is a conversation between the people who own the value (PO) and the people who own the work (Developers). Stakeholders and a 'project manager' aren't part of it.

text: A Scrum Team is a cohesive unit of professionals that consists of which of the following? (choose all that apply)
options: Developers.
One Product Owner.
Users.
One Scrum Master.
Customers.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: Developers, one Product Owner, and one Scrum Master. That is the whole Scrum Team. Users and customers are stakeholders, not members of the team.

text: Which of the following is required by Scrum? (choose the best answer)
options: Sprint Retrospective.
Developers must stand up at the Daily Scrum.
Sprint Burndown Chart.
Release Planning.
All of the above.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the Sprint Retrospective, a required event. Standing at the Daily Scrum, burndown charts, and Release Planning are optional practices or non-Scrum, not requirements.

text: A Scrum Master is working with a Scrum Team that has Developers in different physical locations. The Developers meet in a variety of meeting rooms and have much to do logistically (for example: reserve meeting rooms and set up conference calls) before the Daily Scrum. What action should the Scrum Master take? (choose the best answer)
options: Set up the meeting and tell the Scrum Team that is how it will be done.
Allow the Developers to self-manage and determine for themselves what to do.
Inform management and ask them to solve it.
Ask the Developers to alternate who is responsible for meeting setup.
trap: The Daily Scrum is for Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal.
explanation: Correct: allow the Developers to self-manage and determine what to do. Logistics for their own event are theirs to organize. Imposing a setup, escalating to management, or dictating a rotation all undercut self-management.

text: What does it mean for a Scrum Team to be cross-functional? (choose the best answer)
options: Developers on the Scrum Team work closely with business analysts, architects, developers, and testers who are not on the team.
The Scrum Team includes skilled individuals who together have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint.
The Scrum Team is a virtual team drawing from separate teams of business analysts, architects, developers, and testers.
The Scrum Team includes not only developers but also business analysts, architects, and testers.
trap: Avoid applying traditional project management assumptions to Scrum.
explanation: Correct: the team includes skilled individuals who together have all the skills to create value each Sprint. Cross-functional is a whole-team capability. It doesn't mean relying on outsiders, drawing from separate specialist teams, or simply having named role-titles on the team.

text: The job of a Product Owner focuses on the following: (choose the best two answers)
options: Clearly communicating project or release status and strategies to customers and stakeholders.
Working with customers and stakeholders to identify the most valuable product requirements.
Being with the Scrum Team all the time, just in case they need me to clarify a requirement.
Writing clear, transparent User Stories.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: clearly communicating status/strategy to customers and stakeholders, and working with them to identify the most valuable requirements. The PO's job centers on value and stakeholder alignment — not sitting with the team full-time 'just in case' or personally writing all user stories.

text: When multiple Scrum Teams are working on the same product, should all of their Increments be integrated every Sprint? (choose the best answer)
options: Yes, but only for Scrum Teams whose work has dependencies.
Yes, in order to accurately inspect what is done.
No, that's far too hard and must be done in a hardening Sprint.
No, each Scrum Team stands alone.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: yes, in order to accurately inspect what is Done. When multiple teams share a product, their work must integrate every Sprint to produce a single, transparent, inspectable Increment. Integrating only dependent teams, or deferring integration to a hardening Sprint, breaks that transparency.

text: Which statement best describes a Product Owner's responsibility? (choose the best answer)
options: Optimizing the value of the work the Scrum Team does.
Keep stakeholders from distracting the Developers.
Directing the Developers.
Ensuring that the work meets the commitments to the stakeholders.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: optimizing the value of the work the Scrum Team does. That is the PO's defining responsibility. They don't shield Developers as a gatekeeper, direct the Developers, or enforce 'commitments to stakeholders'.

text: Which two things should the Scrum Team do during the first Sprint? (choose the best two answers)
options: Make up a plan for the rest of the project.
Create at least one valuable, useful Increment.
Build at least one piece of valuable functionality.
Define the major product features and a release plan architecture.
Analyze, describe, and document the requirements for the subsequent Sprints.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: create at least one valuable, useful Increment, and build at least one piece of valuable functionality. Even the first Sprint must produce value — not an upfront project plan, a documented requirements set for later Sprints, or a release-architecture phase.

text: What is the timebox for the Sprint Planning event? (choose the best answer)
options: Whenever it is done.
Monthly.
4 hours for a one-month Sprint.
8 hours for a one-month Sprint.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: 8 hours for a one-month Sprint. That is the maximum timebox, shorter for shorter Sprints. (4 hours is the Sprint Review's timebox, not Planning's.)

text: Who owns the Sprint Backlog? (choose the best answer)
options: The Product Owner.
The Scrum Team.
The Developers.
The Scrum Master.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: the Developers. They own the Sprint Backlog because they own the plan and the work to meet the Sprint Goal. Not the Product Owner, Scrum Master, or the Scrum Team collectively.

text: Which of the following are appropriate topics for discussion during a Sprint Retrospective? (choose the best two answers)
options: Documenting acceptance criteria for items in the next Sprint.
The order of items in the Product Backlog.
Identifying high priority process improvements for the next Sprint.
How the team collaborates.
trap: Scrum protects the Sprint Goal and the timebox; it does not guarantee all forecast work.
explanation: Correct: identifying high-priority process improvements for the next Sprint, and how the team collaborates. The Retrospective targets team effectiveness and process. Writing acceptance criteria and ordering the Product Backlog are refinement/PO activities, not Retrospective topics.

text: What is the Product Owner responsible for during the Sprint Retrospective? (choose the best answer)
options: Participating as a Scrum Team member.
The Product Owner should not take part in Sprint Retrospective.
Capturing requirements for the Product Backlog.
Summarizing and reporting the discussions to the stakeholders that they represent in the Scrum Team.
trap: Do not confuse Product Owner accountability with stakeholder or Developer decisions.
explanation: Correct: participating as a Scrum Team member. In the Retrospective the PO contributes as part of the team's self-improvement — not sitting out, gathering requirements, or reporting the discussion back to stakeholders.
